lead: Both readings today ask the same question: who is Jesus? Paul answers with an early hymn of the Church: “He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels.” In John the question is put to Jesus directly, “Who are you?”, and he answers that it will become plain when he is lifted up on the cross. The Church, Paul says, is the household that holds up this truth for the world to see. The key words are mystery and lifted up.

r.h: The pillar and bulwark of the truth
set: The First Letter to Timothy is written to Paul's young co-worker, left in charge of the Church at Ephesus (1:3). It gives instructions on prayer, on the qualities of bishops and deacons (3:1–13), and on the life of the community. Many scholars think that the Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) were written in Paul's name by a disciple after his death; others hold that they come from Paul himself, late in his life. Either way, the Church receives them as inspired Scripture.
Today's three verses are the hinge of the letter. Paul explains why he writes, and then breaks into what most scholars take to be a hymn or confession already in use in the Church's worship.
str: vv. 14–15: why he writes: so that Timothy may know how to behave in the household of God.
v. 16: the hymn of the mystery, in six short lines.
¶ The lines come in pairs that join earth and heaven: flesh and spirit, angels and nations, the world and glory.
kw: Not a building but a family. The same letter asks that a bishop manage his own household well, “for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he take care of God's church?” (3:5). The Church is God's family, with its order, its table and its care for the weak.

A pillar holds something up so that it can be seen; a bulwark (foundation, support) keeps it firm. The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was famous for its many pillars. Paul says the true pillar is the Church of the living God, and what she holds up is the truth.
Literally “the mystery of godliness” or “of devotion”. In Paul a mystery is not a riddle but God's plan, once hidden and now revealed in Christ (Colossians 1:26).
vv: you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth.
Conduct comes first. Before he speaks of doctrine, Paul speaks of how people behave in God's house. Truth and life belong together.
Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great:
The Greek word translated “without any doubt” means “by common confession”: what follows is what all believers confess together.
He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels,

The best and oldest manuscripts begin “who was revealed”; some later manuscripts read “God was revealed in flesh”. Both say the same faith: the one revealed in the flesh is the eternal Son. “Vindicated in spirit” points to the Resurrection, in which the Spirit showed him to be righteous.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it speaks of the Church as the guardian of revealed truth: the Church, “the pillar and bulwark of the truth”, faithfully guards the faith handed on once for all to the saints (CCC 171). It also quotes the hymn of verse 16, “the mystery of our religion”, and sees in it the heart of faith in the true Incarnation of the Son of God (CCC 463). The Church does not stand above the truth; she serves it, holds it up and keeps it safe.

r.h: When you have lifted up the Son of Man
set: Jesus is teaching in the temple in Jerusalem during the feast of Tabernacles (7:2, 7:14; 8:20). The conversation in chapter 8 is tense. In John's Gospel “the Jews” in such scenes usually means the religious authorities who opposed Jesus; here the questioners are the Pharisees of 8:13. John himself, like Jesus and the first disciples, was a Jew, and today's passage ends with many of the hearers coming to faith (8:30).
Just before, Jesus has said: “you will die in your sins unless you believe that I am he” (8:24). The question “Who are you?” follows from that.
str: vv. 25–27: “Who are you?”; Jesus speaks of the one who sent him; they do not understand.
vv. 28–29: when the Son of Man is lifted up, they will know that “I am he”.
v. 30: many believe in him.
kw: Literally “I am”. In the Greek Old Testament God speaks of himself with these words: “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he” (Isaiah 43:10). Jesus uses the same words of himself (8:24, 28, 58).
The word means both to raise up and to exalt. In John it always points to the cross, where Jesus is raised up and glorified at the same time (3:14; 12:32–33).
One of John's favourite ways of speaking of the Father. Everything Jesus says and does comes from the Father who sent him.
vv: They said to him, “Who are you?”

Jesus's answer in the Greek is one of the hardest phrases in John. The NRSV renders it as a question, “Why do I speak to you at all?”; other translations, like the POC, read it as “What I have told you from the beginning”. Either way, Jesus will not give a new title. He has already told them.
When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he,
A startling promise: the moment of his deepest humiliation will be the moment his identity shines out. At the cross the centurion in Mark says, “Truly this man was God's Son!” (Mark 15:39).
he has not left me alone, for I always do what is pleasing to him.
Even on the cross Jesus is not abandoned by the Father. His whole life is obedience, and in that obedience he is never alone.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 28 when it teaches about the divine name. God revealed himself to Moses as “I AM”; Jesus reveals that he himself bears that name, and that this will be seen when he is lifted up (CCC 211). The Church therefore reads this passage as a revelation of the divinity of Christ, which is shown most clearly not in power but in the cross.

rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Justin, philosopher and martyr. Born about the year 100 at Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, he searched for truth among the philosophers and found it in Christ. He opened a school in Rome and was beheaded there with several companions around 165. His First Apology gives the oldest full description of the Sunday Eucharist, which the Catechism quotes at length (CCC 1345). Justin is a fitting saint for these readings: he went looking for the answer to the question “Who are you?” and found it in the crucified Lord.
study: Paul calls the Church “the household of God”. How do I behave in God's house, and in my own home, so that the truth can be seen?
Jesus says that people will know who he is when he is lifted up. What does the cross teach me about who Jesus is?

lead: Today's readings are about how God works: not through what the world counts as strong and impressive, but through what looks small and weak. Paul preaches “Christ crucified”, which seems foolish, yet is “the power of God and the wisdom of God”. Jesus compares the kingdom to a tiny mustard seed and to a little yeast hidden in a great mass of flour. The key words are the cross and small beginnings.

r.h: The message about the cross
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, probably around AD 54–55, to a young Church he had founded a few years earlier. Corinth was a rich, proud port city, and the community was splitting into groups that boasted of their favourite teachers: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos” (1:12). Some were attracted by clever speech and philosophy.
Paul answers by going to the root: the Gospel is not a human philosophy to be admired but the message of a crucified Messiah. He quotes Isaiah 29:14 from the Greek Old Testament.
str: v. 18: the message of the cross: foolishness to some, the power of God to others.
vv. 19–21: God overturns the wisdom of the world (Isaiah 29:14).
vv. 22–24: signs, wisdom, and Christ crucified.
v. 25: the foolishness and weakness of God.
kw: Literally “the word of the cross”. Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, kept for slaves and rebels. To preach a crucified man as Lord sounded absurd.
The word is related to our “moron”. Paul uses the very insult that was thrown at Christians and turns it around.
A trap or an obstacle that makes one trip. A crucified Messiah seemed to contradict what many expected of God's anointed one.
vv: For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
Paul does not say “the message about wisdom” or “the message about miracles”. The power of God is found in the cross. The verbs are in the present: salvation is a road on which we are travelling.
but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,

Paul, himself a Jew, describes the two great reactions he met in his preaching. He is not condemning a people; in the next verse he says that the called, “both Jews and Greeks”, find in Christ the power and wisdom of God.
For God’s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and God’s weakness is stronger than human strength.
A bold paradox. God has no foolishness or weakness in himself; Paul means what looks foolish and weak to us, above all the cross.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it speaks of God's almighty power: it is shown most mysteriously in the voluntary humiliation and the Resurrection of his Son, so that Christ crucified is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (CCC 272). The Church does not hide the cross; she places it above the altar and signs every Christian with it.

r.h: The mustard seed and the yeast
set: Luke places these two short parables right after Jesus heals a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years, on a sabbath in a synagogue (13:10–17). The leader of the synagogue was indignant, but “the entire crowd was rejoicing” (13:17). Luke then writes, “He said therefore”: the kingdom is already at work in such small signs. Matthew gives the same two parables together (Matthew 13:31–33).
str: vv. 18–19: the mustard seed that grows into a tree where birds nest.
vv. 20–21: the yeast that leavens three measures of flour.
kw: The black mustard of Palestine has a tiny seed, proverbial for smallness, yet it can grow into a large shrub, as tall as a man or more.
Usually an image of corruption in the Bible (Luke 12:1; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here Jesus surprises his hearers by using it for the kingdom.
A very large quantity of flour, enough to make bread for a great crowd. Sarah used the same amount when she baked for the three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18:6).
vv: What is the kingdom of God like? And to what should I compare it?
Jesus looks for images from everyday life. The kingdom cannot be defined in one sentence; it is shown in pictures that set us thinking.
it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.
The words echo Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4, where a great tree shelters every kind of bird, a picture of a kingdom that gives shelter to the nations. The small seed becomes a home for many.
It is like yeast that a woman took and mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.
The Greek verb translated “mixed in” means literally “hid”. The yeast works unseen, from within, until the whole is changed.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is on earth “the initial budding forth” of the kingdom, and that while she slowly grows she longs for the completed kingdom (Lumen Gentium 5). St Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke, sees Christ himself in the mustard seed, small and despised, buried in the earth, and rising to give shelter to all (in substance). The parables give courage to small parishes, to families and to all who think their faithfulness makes no difference.

qa: If the Church is the beginning of the kingdom, why does she look so weak and small in many places?

Because God's way is the way of the mustard seed and the yeast. The kingdom grows hidden, from within, often through what seems insignificant: a family praying, a teacher's patience, a sick person offering suffering. Its growth is God's work, not a matter of numbers. Paul says the same in today's Epistle: God's weakness is stronger than human strength.
study: Where in my life have I been tempted to trust in what looks impressive rather than in the cross?
What small seed of faith or kindness can I sow today, trusting God to make it grow?

lead: In this week after Pentecost both readings speak of the Spirit. Paul tells the Galatians that Christ took our curse upon himself “so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.” Jesus warns that a soul emptied of evil but left empty is in danger: the house must be filled. The key words are blessing and the filled house.

r.h: Blessed with Abraham who believed
set: Paul writes to the Churches of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey, probably in the mid-50s AD. After he left, other teachers had come and told the Gentile converts that to belong fully to God's people they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul answers that they received the Spirit not by works of the law but by believing the Gospel (3:2–5).

Today's verses form a chain of Old Testament texts: Genesis 12:3 and 18:18 (the blessing of the nations), Deuteronomy 27:26 (the curse), Habakkuk 2:4 (the righteous live by faith), Leviticus 18:5 (life by doing the law) and Deuteronomy 21:23 (one hanged on a tree). Paul argues as a trained Jewish teacher, from Scripture to Scripture.
str: vv. 7–9: the children of Abraham are those who believe; the nations are blessed in him.
vv. 10–12: the law, taken alone, cannot give life and leaves us under a curse.
vv. 13–14: Christ became a curse for us, so that the blessing and the Spirit come to all.
kw: Trust in God and his promise, as Abraham trusted (3:6; Genesis 15:6). For Paul faith is never idle: elsewhere in this letter he speaks of “faith working through love” (5:6).

The observances of the Mosaic law, such as circumcision and the food laws, when they are made the condition for belonging to God's people apart from Christ. Paul calls the law itself holy (Romans 7:12).
To buy out, to ransom, as a slave is bought out of slavery. Christ paid the price for us with his own life.
vv: so, you see, those who believe are the descendants of Abraham.
Abraham's true family is not only a matter of birth. Abraham himself believed God before he was circumcised (Romans 4:10–11).
Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law; for “The one who is righteous will live by faith.”
Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4. In Hebrew the word means faithfulness, steady trust in God. Paul hears in it the way of faith opened in Christ.
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us
Deuteronomy 21:23 says that one hanged on a tree is under God's curse. Paul sees the cross in that light: Jesus took the place of the cursed, so that we might receive the blessing.
so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.
The promise made to Abraham reaches its goal at Pentecost: the gift of the Holy Spirit poured out on Jews and Gentiles alike.
ch: The Church teaches that justification has been merited for us by the Passion of Christ and is given through Baptism, the sacrament of faith (CCC 1992). Faith is the beginning of salvation, and the works that follow are themselves the fruit of grace, done in Christ and by his Spirit. Paul is not teaching that the law of Moses was evil or that God has rejected his people; the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). He teaches that in Christ the blessing promised to Abraham is opened to every nation.

r.h: The house swept and put in order
set: These verses close a controversy. Jesus has cast out a demon, and some say he does it by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons (11:14–15). He answers that he casts out demons “by the finger of God” (11:20), and that “Whoever is not with me is against me” (11:23). Then comes this short warning. Right after it a woman calls out a blessing on his mother, and Jesus answers: “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!” (11:28). Matthew has the same saying (Matthew 12:43–45).
str: v. 24: the unclean spirit leaves, wanders, and decides to return.
v. 25: it finds the house swept and put in order.
v. 26: it brings seven worse spirits, and the last state is worse than the first.
kw: Rest, a place to settle. The evil spirit finds no rest in the desert and looks for a human heart to live in.
Clean and tidy, but in Matthew's version also “empty” (Matthew 12:44). Nothing new has come to live in the house.
The number of fullness in the Bible. The danger is not a small one but complete.
vv: it wanders through waterless regions looking for a resting place,
In the thinking of the time the desert was a place of evil spirits. The image is of a restless power that does not give up easily.
When it comes, it finds it swept and put in order.
Being cleaned is not enough. A life from which sin has been driven out must be filled with God, or it will be filled again by something worse.
and the last state of that person is worse than the first.
A warning against half-hearted conversion: to turn away from evil without turning towards Christ.
ch: The Church teaches that conversion is not only a first step at Baptism but a continual task for the whole Church and for each Christian, a “second conversion” that lasts a lifetime (CCC 1428). The context shows how the house is filled: by hearing the word of God and keeping it (11:28), and, in this season, by the Holy Spirit, who comes to dwell in those who belong to Christ.

study: Paul says that Christ became a curse for us. How does that change the way I look at my own sins and at the cross?
After I have confessed a sin, how do I fill the “swept house” with prayer, the word of God and good works?

lead: For the memory of a bishop the Church reads of faithful leaders. Hebrews asks us to remember those who spoke the word of God to us and to imitate their faith, and leads us to Jesus who suffered outside the gate and to the altar where we share in his sacrifice. In Matthew the Lord asks who is the faithful and wise servant, set over the household to give food at the proper time. Three alternative Gospels are also given: the good shepherd who lays down his life (John 10:11–18), the way, the truth and the life (John 14:1–6), and the greatest love (John 15:9–17). The key words are remember, the altar and faithful.

r.h: Remember your leaders
set: The Letter to the Hebrews was written to Christians, probably of Jewish background, who were tired and tempted to drift away. Its author is not named. The Church long counted it among the letters of Paul; most scholars today think it was written by another teacher of the apostolic generation, and the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. Chapter 13 gathers final counsels.

Throughout the letter the author has compared the sacrifices of the old covenant with the one sacrifice of Christ. Here he recalls the Day of Atonement, when the bodies of the animals offered for sin were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27).
str: vv. 7–8: remember your leaders; Jesus Christ is the same for ever.
v. 9: do not be carried away by strange teachings.
vv. 10–14: our altar; Jesus suffered outside the gate; let us go out to him.
vv. 15–16: the sacrifice of praise and the sacrifice of sharing.
kw: Those who lead and guide the community. The word returns in 13:17 and 13:24. Those of verse 7 seem to have already died, since their “outcome” can be seen.
The place of sacrifice. The author speaks of an altar from which the priests of the old tent have no right to eat: the sacrifice of Christ and the table where his people share in it.
Jesus was crucified outside the walls of Jerusalem (John 19:17, 20), like the sin offering burned outside the camp.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
Remembering is more than gratitude. We look at how a shepherd's life ended, and we imitate his faith, not only his works.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Leaders come and go; Christ remains. The bishop who taught us pointed to one who does not change.
We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.
Many Catholic interpreters see here both the cross and the Eucharistic table that makes the sacrifice of the cross present. The Christian altar is not a table of ordinary food.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood.
What the old sin offering pointed to, Christ fulfilled. To go “outside the camp” with him (13:13) is to share his rejection and his love.
Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God,
Praise and sharing (13:16) are called sacrifices. They do not replace the sacrifice of Christ; they flow from it and are offered “through him”.
ch: The Catechism names the Eucharist among other titles “the sacrifice of praise”, quoting Hebrews 13:15 (CCC 1330). It also teaches that the altar of the New Covenant is the Lord's cross, from which the sacraments of the Paschal mystery flow (CCC 1182). So the Church reads these verses at the memory of a bishop: the shepherd is remembered at the altar where he offered the Holy Qurbono, and his people are asked to imitate his faith.

r.h: The faithful and wise slave
set: These verses belong to the last great discourse of Jesus in Matthew (chapters 24–25), spoken on the Mount of Olives a few days before his Passion. He has just said that no one knows the day or the hour (24:36) and that the disciples must keep awake (24:42). This parable is the first of several on readiness, followed by the ten bridesmaids and the talents (25:1–30). Luke has a similar parable (Luke 12:42–46).
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise slave?
vv. 46–47: the blessing of the one found at work.
vv. 48–51: the wicked slave who says “My master is delayed”.
kw: Faithful: one who can be trusted. Wise: one who sees what the hour demands. The same pair is used of the wise bridesmaids in 25:2.
The master's household servants. The steward does not own them; he is set over them to serve them.
A word Matthew often uses. In Luke's version the place is with “the unfaithful” (Luke 12:46).
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household,
The steward's task is to give the others their food “at the proper time”. Authority in the Lord's household is service: feeding others with the word and the sacraments.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
The master does not ask for spectacular deeds but for faithfulness in the ordinary task he has given.
But if that wicked slave says to himself, ‘My master is delayed,’

The danger begins in the heart, with the thought that there is no hurry. Then come harshness to others and self-indulgence. The severe ending (24:51) uses the strong language of judgment to show how serious it is to abuse the trust of the Lord.
ch: The Second Vatican Council asks the bishop to keep before his eyes the example of the Good Shepherd, who came not to be served but to serve and to lay down his life for his sheep (Lumen Gentium 27). This parable, and the alternative Gospel of the good shepherd, describe what the Church hopes for in every bishop and priest, and what every Christian is asked within his own household.

qa: Does the “sacrifice of praise” mean that Christians no longer need the sacrifice of the altar?

No. Hebrews says “We have an altar”. Our praise, our good works and our sharing are offered “through him”, that is, through Christ and his one sacrifice, which is made present in the Holy Qurbono. The Catechism calls the Eucharist itself the sacrifice of praise (CCC 1330). Our spiritual sacrifices are joined to his offering; they do not take its place.
rite: The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Most Rev. Geevarghese Mar Timotheos, a bishop of our Church who went to the Lord in 2019, with the readings appointed for the memory of a bishop. It is also the First Friday, when many families go to confession and receive Holy Communion, and June has long been kept by Catholics in Kerala as the month of the Sacred Heart; the Latin Church celebrates that solemnity today. Hebrews brings these together: we remember a shepherd and pray for him, and we go out to Jesus who sanctified the people “by his own blood”.
study: Whom do I remember as a leader who spoke the word of God to me? What in their faith can I imitate?
In the household the Lord has given me, my family, parish or work, whom am I asked to feed “at the proper time”?

lead: Both readings today are about the Scriptures. Paul reminds Timothy that he has known the sacred writings from childhood and that “All scripture is inspired by God.” In the Gospel Jesus himself reads a psalm with authority and shows that the Messiah is not only David's son but David's Lord. The key words are inspired and Lord.

r.h: All scripture is inspired by God
set: The Second Letter to Timothy presents itself as Paul's last letter, written in chains in Rome (1:8, 1:17) when he knows that “the time of my departure has come” (4:6). As with the other Pastoral Letters, many scholars think a disciple wrote it in Paul's name; others defend Paul's own authorship. It reads as a testament, a father's words to his son in the faith.

Antioch (in Pisidia), Iconium and Lystra are the towns of Paul's first missionary journey, where he was driven out and at Lystra stoned and left for dead (Acts 13–14). Lystra was Timothy's own home town (Acts 16:1), so he may have seen these things with his own eyes.
str: vv. 10–11: Timothy has followed Paul's teaching and life, and his sufferings.
vv. 12–13: all who want to live a godly life will be persecuted; impostors will go from bad to worse.
vv. 14–15: continue in what you have learned; you have known the sacred writings from childhood.
vv. 16–17: all Scripture is inspired by God and equips the person of God.
kw: Literally “you have followed closely”. Timothy learned the faith not only from words but by watching how Paul lived and suffered.
The Scriptures of Israel, which Christians call the Old Testament. Timothy learned them from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (1:5).
Literally “God-breathed”. The word is found only here in the New Testament. Scripture comes from the breath of God, the same breath that gave life to the first man (Genesis 2:7).
vv: Indeed, all who want to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.
Paul does not promise an easy life. Faithfulness to Christ always meets resistance, whether open persecution or quiet mockery.
continue in what you have learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it,
Faith is received from people we can trust. Knowing who taught us helps us to stand firm when new teachers come.
All scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness,

Four uses: to teach the truth, to show what is wrong, to set it right, and to form a righteous life. Scripture is given not only to be studied but to make us “proficient, equipped for every good work” (3:17).
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse when it teaches that the books of Scripture, written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, have God as their author, and teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth God wished to be recorded for the sake of our salvation (Dei Verbum 11; CCC 105–107). The Catechism also recalls the saying of St Jerome: “Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ” (CCC 133).

r.h: David himself calls him Lord
set: Jesus is teaching in the temple during the last days before his Passion. Mark has just told of a series of questions put to him: about taxes, about the resurrection, and about the greatest commandment (12:13–34). After the scribe who agreed with him, “no one dared to ask him any question” (12:34). Now Jesus asks a question of his own.

He quotes Psalm 110:1, a royal psalm traditionally ascribed to David. It is the Old Testament verse most often quoted or echoed in the New Testament. Peter uses it on the day of Pentecost to proclaim the risen Jesus as Lord (Acts 2:34–36).
str: v. 35: the question: how can the scribes say the Messiah is the son of David?
v. 36: David, by the Holy Spirit, calls him “my Lord” (Psalm 110:1).
v. 37: so how can he be his son? The crowd listens with delight.
kw: The Anointed One. Many in Israel expected the Messiah to be a descendant of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16).
In the Hebrew of the psalm the first “Lord” is the divine name and the second is ’adōnî, “my lord”. The Greek uses kyrios for both. David calls the Messiah his lord.
Jesus treats the psalm as words spoken under the Holy Spirit, which agrees with today's Epistle: all Scripture is inspired by God.
vv: How can the scribes say that the Messiah is the son of David?
Jesus does not deny that the Messiah is David's son. Mark has told us that blind Bartimaeus called him “Son of David” (10:47), and Jesus accepted it. He shows that the title says too little.
David himself, by the Holy Spirit, declared,
The king of Israel speaks of someone greater than himself, who will sit at the right hand of God. A father did not call his son “lord”. So the Messiah must be more than a son of David.
David himself calls him Lord; so how can he be his son?
The answer is the mystery of Christ: by his birth he is son of David, and as the eternal Son he is David's Lord. Jesus leaves the question open for his hearers to ponder.
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus ascribes the title “Lord” to himself in a veiled way when he disputes about Psalm 110 (CCC 447), and it teaches that being seated at the right hand of the Father means the beginning of the Messiah's kingdom (CCC 664). The Creed says the same: he “is seated at the right hand of the Father”.

rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Boniface, bishop and martyr, the apostle of the Germans. Born in Wessex in England about 675 and first named Wynfrith, he became a monk and then a missionary among the Germanic peoples, was made archbishop, and founded monasteries and dioceses. He was killed with his companions at Dokkum in Frisia in 754, while preparing to confirm new Christians. Like Timothy, he had learned the Scriptures from childhood, in his case in a monastery, and he carried them with him to the end.
study: From whom did I first learn the Scriptures? How can I hand them on to the children in my home and parish?
Jesus calls himself David's Lord. In what part of my life do I still need to let Jesus be Lord?

lead: On the Third Sunday after Pentecost the readings speak of hunger and bread, of guilt and forgiveness, and of a faith that stays firm. In the evening Gospel (Mark 6:4–13) Jesus is not honoured in his home town, yet he sends the Twelve out two by two; they preach repentance and anoint the sick with oil. Judges 1:8–11 tells how the people of Judah went up to take the land. In Daniel 3:1–18 three young men refuse to worship the golden statue: “But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods.” In Jeremiah 3:1–5 the Lord confronts an unfaithful people who still call him “My Father”. In Acts 13:26–41 Paul preaches at Antioch in Pisidia: “through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you.”

We study three readings more closely. In Genesis, Joseph's brothers come to Egypt for grain in a famine and, without knowing it, stand before the brother they sold; for the first time they admit their guilt. Paul ends his letter to the Galatians in his own large handwriting: he will boast only in the cross, for “a new creation is everything!” In John, Jesus says, “I am the bread of life”, and promises that whoever comes to him will never be driven away. The key words are bread, the cross and drawn.

r.h: We are paying the penalty for what we did to our brother
set: The story of Joseph fills the last chapters of Genesis (37–50). Years earlier his brothers, jealous of their father's love for him, threw him into a pit and sold him to traders going down to Egypt (37:18–28). In Egypt, after slavery and prison, Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dreams, foresaw seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and was set over the land to store grain (41).

Now the famine has reached Canaan, and Jacob sends ten of his sons to buy grain. They bow before the governor of Egypt without recognising him. Joseph recognises them. He speaks harshly, accuses them of being spies and keeps them in custody for three days (42:6–17). Today's verses follow. Joseph is testing them: have they changed? Will they abandon another brother as they abandoned him?
str: vv. 18–20: Joseph's new terms: one brother stays bound; the rest take grain home and bring back Benjamin.
vv. 21–22: the brothers confess their guilt for what they did to Joseph; Reuben recalls his warning.
vv. 23–24: Joseph, who understands them, turns away and weeps; Simeon is bound before their eyes.
v. 25: their sacks are filled with grain and each man's money is secretly returned.
¶ The scene moves from fear to conscience, and from conscience towards the reconciliation of chapter 45.
kw: Joseph tells them, without revealing who he is, that he fears God. In Genesis the fear of God is the root of right conduct (compare 20:11). The brothers, who once showed no pity, are now in the hands of a man who does.
The brothers say literally “truly we are guilty”. The word is used for guilt that must be answered for. About twenty years later their conscience wakes.
Joseph speaks through an interpreter, so the brothers think he cannot understand them. Their private confession is heard by the very one they wronged.
vv: Do this and you will live, for I fear God:
Joseph softens his first demand that one brother go and the rest stay in prison (42:16). The one who holds their life in his hands chooses mercy.
Alas, we are paying the penalty for what we did to our brother; we saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen.

The first time Genesis tells us that Joseph pleaded with them from the pit is here, in the brothers' own confession. Guilt long buried rises when trouble comes. True repentance begins when we see the anguish of the one we hurt.
They did not know that Joseph understood them, since he spoke with them through an interpreter.
God hears even what we think no one hears. The brothers' confession is not spoken to Joseph, yet it reaches him.
He turned away from them and wept;
This is the first of several times Joseph weeps (43:30; 45:2, 14–15; 50:17). His harshness is a test, not revenge. Behind the stern face of the governor is a brother's heart.
to return every man’s money to his sack,
A hidden gift. The brothers will be frightened when they find it (42:28), but it is a sign of grace: they receive bread without paying for it.
ch: The Fathers often saw in Joseph a figure of Christ: rejected and sold by his brothers, humbled and then raised up, he feeds the hungry and forgives those who wronged him. St Ambrose wrote a whole work, On Joseph, in this spirit. The Catechism quotes Joseph's later words to his brothers, “You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good”, to show how God's providence can draw good even from sin (CCC 312; Genesis 50:20). The bread that Joseph gives in the famine points to the bread of life in today's Gospel.

r.h: A new creation is everything
set: These verses close Paul's letter to the Galatians. Throughout the letter he has argued that Gentile believers do not need to be circumcised in order to belong fully to God's people, because they have received the Spirit through faith in Christ. Some teachers were urging circumcision on them.

At verse 11 Paul takes the pen from the scribe who wrote the letter at his dictation and adds a final paragraph in his own hand, as he does elsewhere (1 Corinthians 16:21; 2 Thessalonians 3:17). The dispute is among believers in Christ about what to ask of Gentile converts; it is not an attack on the Jewish people, to whom Paul himself belonged.
str: v. 10: let us do good to all, especially to the family of faith.
v. 11: Paul writes in his own hand.
vv. 12–13: the motives of those who urge circumcision.
vv. 14–15: Paul boasts only in the cross; what counts is a new creation.
kw: The right time, the moment given by God. While we have time, we are to do good.
To glory in, to put one's confidence in. Paul refuses to glory in anything that he or others can achieve, only in what Christ has done on the cross.
The same words appear in 2 Corinthians 5:17: “if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation”. In Christ God begins again what he began in Genesis.
vv: let us work for the good of all, and especially for those of the family of faith.
Charity has no limits, “the good of all”, yet the Church is a family with a special duty to its own members, above all the poor among them.
See what large letters I make when I am writing in my own hand!
Some think the large letters show Paul's poor eyesight (compare 4:15); others that he writes large for emphasis. Either way, the apostle signs his letter with his own hand and his own heart.
May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
The cross, once a sign of shame, has become Paul's only glory. Through it the old world of pride and rivalry has lost its hold on him.
but a new creation is everything!
Neither being circumcised nor being uncircumcised makes a person new. Only God's grace does, given in Baptism and lived by the Spirit.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Baptism makes the neophyte “a new creature”, an adopted son of God and a partaker of the divine nature (CCC 1265). The Church signs the Christian with the cross at Baptism and at every blessing, so that Paul's words become our own: our glory is the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

r.h: I am the bread of life
set: Chapter 6 of John begins with the feeding of the five thousand near the Sea of Galilee, when the Passover was near (6:4). The next day the crowd finds Jesus at Capernaum (6:24, 59). They ask for a sign and recall that their ancestors ate manna in the wilderness (6:30–31). Jesus answers that the true bread from heaven is given by his Father, and then says plainly: “I am the bread of life.”

Many interpreters see two movements in the discourse. In verses 35–50 Jesus is the bread to be received by faith: whoever comes to him and believes. From verse 51 he speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood, words the Church has always understood of the Eucharist. Today's passage belongs to the first part. In verse 41 John says “the Jews” began to complain; here the term stands for the hearers in the synagogue at Capernaum who could not accept his claim, not for the Jewish people as such. Jesus, his disciples and many who believed in him were Jews.
str: v. 35: “I am the bread of life”: whoever comes and believes will not hunger or thirst.
vv. 36–40: the Father's will: that none be lost, and that all who believe have eternal life and be raised on the last day.
vv. 41–42: the hearers complain: is he not the son of Joseph?
vv. 43–46: no one can come unless drawn by the Father; all shall be taught by God.
kw: egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs
I am the bread of life

The first of the great “I am” sayings in John with an image: bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine. Bread is the food of every day and of every home. Jesus gives himself as that which keeps us alive.
To murmur, to grumble. It recalls how Israel complained in the wilderness before the manna was given (Exodus 16:2, 7–8).
The Father “draws” people to Jesus. John uses the same verb when Jesus says that, lifted up on the cross, he will draw all people to himself (12:32). Faith is God's gift before it is our act.
vv: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
“Comes” and “believes” say the same thing in two ways. The hunger meant is the deep hunger of the heart, which no other food can satisfy.
anyone who comes to me I will never drive away;
One of the most consoling verses of the Gospel. No one who comes to Jesus, however weak or sinful, will be turned out.
This is indeed the will of my Father, that all who see the Son and believe in him may have eternal life; and I will raise them up on the last day.
The promise “I will raise them up on the last day” returns four times in this chapter (6:39, 40, 44, 54). Eternal life begins now in faith and is completed in the resurrection of the body.
Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?

The hearers think they know where he comes from. They see only his earthly family, not that he has come down from heaven. The evening Gospel tells the same story in his home town: familiarity becomes a stumbling block.
No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me;

This does not mean that God draws some and refuses others. The Church teaches that God wills all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), and the next verse explains how the Father draws: by teaching every heart that listens.
And they shall all be taught by God.
Jesus recalls the prophets, especially Isaiah 54:13: “All your children shall be taught by the Lord.” In the new covenant God himself teaches his people from within, by his Spirit.
ch: The Catechism teaches that St John reports the words of Jesus in the synagogue at Capernaum which prepare for the institution of the Eucharist: Christ calls himself the bread of life, come down from heaven (CCC 1338). It also teaches that faith is a gift of God, a supernatural virtue infused by him, and at the same time a truly human act (CCC 153–154). St Augustine, preaching on verse 44, says that the Father draws us not by force but by delight, as a sheep is drawn by a green branch held out to it (Tractates on John 26, in substance). The promise of resurrection “on the last day” is taught in CCC 1001.

qa: If no one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws him, are some people simply not chosen?

No. The Church teaches that God “desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). The Father's drawing is the grace offered to every human heart. Jesus himself explains it in the next verse: everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to him. We can resist that grace, but we can never come to Christ without it. That is why we pray for those who do not yet believe.
Why did Joseph treat his brothers so harshly if he loved them?

Joseph was testing whether they had changed. About twenty years earlier they had sold a brother and lied to their father. Now he sees whether they will abandon Simeon and Benjamin in the same way. The test leads them to confess their guilt, and in chapter 44 Judah offers himself as a slave in place of Benjamin. Joseph's tears (42:24) show that his heart was never closed. Forgiveness does not ignore the truth; it helps the guilty to face it and be healed.
Is the bread of life only faith in Jesus, or is it the Eucharist?

Both, and they belong together. In the first part of the discourse Jesus is received by faith; from verse 51 he speaks of giving his flesh to eat. The Church has always read the whole chapter in the light of the Eucharist (CCC 1338). We come to the Holy Qurbono first by believing, and in receiving the Body and Blood of Christ our faith is fed.
rite: In the West Syriac tradition the Sundays after Pentecost unfold the life of the Church that the Spirit has gathered. This Sunday's readings are full of signs of that life: the Twelve sent out two by two, the anointing of the sick with oil, which the Catechism sees as a hint of the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick (CCC 1511; Mark 6:13), forgiveness proclaimed through Jesus, and the bread of life. In every Holy Qurbono the Malankara faithful receive the bread that came down from heaven. Like Joseph in the famine, the Church does not keep the bread for herself: she gives it to all who come hungry, and Jesus promises that whoever comes will never be driven away.
study: Joseph's brothers remembered their guilt only when trouble came. Is there a wrong I have done that I have buried and need to bring to the sacrament of Reconciliation?
Paul says, “May I never boast of anything except the cross.” What do I secretly boast in, and how can the cross release me from it?
What hunger do I bring to Jesus, the bread of life, when I come to the Holy Qurbono?
Jesus promises never to drive away anyone who comes to him. Is there someone in my family or parish who feels driven away, and how can I help them come back?

lead: Today's two readings are about the community the Lord leaves behind him and what holds it together. The Epistle sets the order of prayer in the church at Ephesus: hands lifted up to God without anger or argument, lives adorned not with display but with good works. In the Gospel, at the Last Supper, Jesus promises the Advocate, who will teach the disciples and remind them of all he has said, and he leaves them his own peace as a parting gift. The key words are prayer and peace.

r.h: Lifting up holy hands
set: The First Letter to Timothy presents itself as Paul's instruction to his co-worker Timothy, whom he had left at Ephesus to stop certain people from teaching a different doctrine (1:3). With 2 Timothy and Titus it is called a Pastoral Letter. Many scholars think these letters were written after Paul's death by a disciple who wrote in his name and spirit; others hold that Paul wrote them late in his life. The Church receives them in either case as inspired Scripture.

Chapter 2 begins with prayer for everyone, for kings and all in authority, because God “desires everyone to be saved” (2:4). Our verses then turn to how men and women bear themselves in the assembly at prayer. The letter is fighting false teachers who, among other things, “forbid marriage” (4:3), and it speaks of some who went from house to house “saying what they should not say” (5:13). That background helps in reading verses 11–15.
str: v. 8: the men: prayer with holy hands, without anger or argument.
vv. 9–10: the women: adorned not with costly display but with good works.
vv. 11–12: learning in quietness; a woman is not to teach or to have authority over a man in the assembly.
vv. 13–14: the reason given from Genesis 2–3.
v. 15: salvation through childbearing, with faith, love and holiness.
¶ The passage is not a complete teaching on men and women. It is a set of directions for one church at prayer, under pressure from false teaching, and it must be read with the rest of Scripture.
kw: Standing with hands raised was the ordinary posture of prayer for Jews and the first Christians; the paintings of the catacombs show the praying figure, the orans, in this way. Holy hands are hands not stained by wrongdoing, and the verse adds “without anger or argument”: prayer is spoiled by quarrels (compare Matthew 5:23–24).

The same family of words appears in 2:2, where the whole church is to lead “a quiet and peaceable life”. It means a calm and settled spirit, not only the absence of speech. In a church disturbed by arguments, the letter asks for a learning that is attentive and peaceable.

A rare verb, found only here in the New Testament. Scholars discuss its exact shade of meaning: some take it simply as “to exercise authority”, others as “to domineer”. In context it concerns the public teaching office in the assembly.
vv: I desire, then, that in every place the men should pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or argument;

“In every place” recalls Malachi 1:11, where the Lord foresees a pure offering made to his name among the nations; the Didache already applied that verse to the Eucharist. Wherever the Church gathers, prayer rises to God.
but with good works, as is proper for women who profess reverence for God.
The true ornament is a life of charity. 1 Peter 3:4 says the same of “the lasting beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit”.
Yet she will be saved through childbearing, provided they continue in faith and love and holiness, with modesty.

A difficult verse. Some interpreters hear in “the childbearing” the birth of the Child promised in Genesis 3:15, through whom salvation comes. Others read it of the vocation of motherhood, lived in faith, against teachers who despised marriage (4:3). In either reading salvation is joined to faith, love and holiness; it is never a merely bodily matter.
ch: The Church reads these verses within the whole of Scripture. Man and woman are created in perfect equality as human persons, each in the image of God (CCC 369; 2334), and Paul writes that in Christ “all of you are one” (Galatians 3:28). St John Paul II's letter Mulieris Dignitatem (1988) reads Genesis and Paul in this light. The Church also holds that priestly ordination is reserved to men, following the choice of Christ and the Apostles (CCC 1577; Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994), and it is in the setting of the liturgical assembly that she has understood the instruction about teaching. At the same time women have always taught the faith: mothers and catechists, foundresses of religious families, and the women Doctors of the Church, St Teresa of Avila and St Catherine of Siena (1970), St Thérèse of Lisieux (1997) and St Hildegard of Bingen (2012).

r.h: Peace I leave with you
set: These verses come from Jesus' farewell discourse at the Last Supper (John 13–17). Judas has gone out into the night (13:30); Jesus has told the disciples that he is going away, and they are troubled. The chapter opened with “Do not let your hearts be troubled” (14:1), and here, near its end, the same words return (14:27). Between them stands the promise of the Advocate. A few verses later Jesus says, “Rise, let us be on our way” (14:31).
str: v. 25: what Jesus has said while he is still with them.
v. 26: the Advocate, sent by the Father in Jesus' name, will teach and remind.
v. 27: the gift of his peace; do not be troubled or afraid.
kw: Literally “one called to the side”: a helper, a defender in court. Among the Gospels only John uses the word (14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7), and 1 John 2:1 uses it of Jesus himself. That is why the Spirit is called “another Advocate” (14:16).

The Spirit does not bring a new Gospel. He brings back to mind what Jesus said and opens its meaning. John notes that the disciples understood some of Jesus' words only after the Resurrection (2:22; 12:16).

Behind it stands the Hebrew šālôm: wholeness, well-being, right relations with God and with one another. It was also the ordinary greeting and farewell. Jesus turns the farewell into a gift: “my peace”.
vv: But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything,

Father, Son and Spirit are named in one sentence: the Father sends the Spirit in the name of the Son. The Church's teaching office lives from this promise; it is not above the word of God but serves it (Dei Verbum 10).
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives.

The world's peace is often a truce, or the quiet of having enough. Christ's peace can live in the middle of trouble, because it rests on him. On Easter evening his first word to the disciples is “Peace be with you” (20:19).
ch: The Church sees in these verses the promise on which her living Tradition rests: the Spirit keeps the memory of Christ alive and leads the Church into a deeper understanding of it (CCC 243; 729). Every liturgy is such a remembering. In the Holy Qurbono the peace is given at the beginning of the anaphora: it passes from the altar to the people and from one to another, a gift received before it is shared. The Catechism calls earthly peace “the image and fruit of the peace of Christ” (CCC 2305).

qa: Does the Holy Spirit teach new things beyond what Jesus taught?

Not in the sense of a new revelation. Christ is the Father's one, perfect and final Word, and there will be no new public revelation before his glorious return (CCC 65–66). What the Spirit gives is understanding: he “will remind you of all that I have said to you” (14:26), so that the Church grows in grasping the full meaning of what was given once for all (CCC 94).
study: Paul asks for prayer “without anger or argument”. Is there a quarrel I need to settle before I lift up my hands at the Holy Qurbono?
Jesus says, “I do not give to you as the world gives.” Where do I usually look for peace, and what would it mean to receive his?

lead: Both readings speak of witness. Paul, in the sharpest quarrel of his ministry, bears witness to the heart of the Gospel: we are made right with God not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. In the Gospel Jesus promises the Spirit of truth, who will testify on his behalf, and tells the disciples, “You also are to testify.” Today the Church remembers St Mariam Thresia, whose whole life was that kind of testimony. The key words are justified and testify.

r.h: Justified through faith in Jesus Christ
set: Paul wrote to the churches of Galatia, in central Asia Minor, probably in the mid-50s. Teachers had come there insisting that Gentile Christians must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to belong fully to God's people. In chapter 2 Paul tells how, at Antioch, Peter used to eat with Gentile believers but drew back when “certain people came from James” (2:12), and how Paul opposed him “to his face” (2:11). Today's verses begin as Paul's words to Peter and flow into his teaching to the Galatians.
str: v. 15: “We ourselves are Jews by birth”: Paul speaks as a Jew to a Jew.
v. 16: justified not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, said three times over.
v. 17: an objection: is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not.
v. 18: to build up again what one has torn down is to become a transgressor.
kw: To declare and make righteous, to set a person in right relationship with God. For Paul it is God's act, received in faith. The Council of Trent teaches that justification is not only the forgiveness of sins but also the sanctification and renewal of the inner person (Decree on Justification, ch. 7).

The deeds the law of Moses requires. In this letter Paul has in view above all those that marked off Jews from Gentiles: circumcision, the food laws, the feasts (2:12; 4:10; 5:2). His point is not that the law is bad; in Romans 7:12 he calls it holy. His point is that no one becomes righteous before God by keeping it.

The Greek can mean “faith in Jesus Christ” or “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ”, and scholars discuss which Paul intends here. The two belong together: Christ's faithfulness to the Father, even to the cross, is what our faith rests on.
vv: yet we know that a person is justified not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.
“We know”: Paul presents this as ground he shares with Peter, not as his own invention. The verse ends with an echo of Psalm 143:2: “no one living is righteous before you.”
is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
If Jewish believers who eat with Gentiles are counted “sinners” by the standard of the law, has Christ led them into sin? Paul refuses the conclusion with his strongest “no”.
But if I build up again the very things that I once tore down, then I demonstrate that I am a transgressor.

What was torn down is the law used as a wall between Jew and Gentile at Christ's table (compare Ephesians 2:14). To build it again, as Peter's withdrawal did, would be to say that faith in Christ was not enough.
ch: The Church teaches with Paul that justification is God's gift, merited for us by the Passion of Christ and given in Baptism (CCC 1987; 1992). No one can merit the first grace of forgiveness and justification; moved by the Holy Spirit, we can then, by grace, do works that are fruitful for eternal life (CCC 2008; 2010). The Council of Trent says that we are justified by faith because faith is the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification (Decree on Justification, ch. 8). In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, confessing together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God.

r.h: The Spirit of truth will testify
set: Still at the Last Supper, Jesus has just warned the disciples that the world will hate them as it hated him (15:18–25). Into that warning he sets the promise of a witness: the Advocate. The next verses speak of being put out of the synagogues and of persecution (16:1–4). The testimony of the Spirit and the testimony of the disciples belong to the time of trial.
str: v. 26: the Advocate, sent by Jesus from the Father, the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father, will testify to Jesus.
v. 27: the disciples also testify, because they have been with him from the beginning.
kw: The Creed of Constantinople (381) took up this word: the Spirit “proceeds from the Father”. The Eastern tradition stresses that the Father is the first source; the Latin tradition adds “and the Son” (Filioque). The Catholic Church teaches that the two ways of speaking, rightly understood, are complementary and do not affect the identity of the one faith (CCC 246–248).
A courtroom word: to bear witness. From the same root comes the word “martyr”: one who bears witness to Christ with his life.

From the start of Jesus' ministry. When the apostles choose a successor for Judas, he must be one who was with them from the baptism of John (Acts 1:21–22). The apostolic witness rests on having been with the Lord.
vv: the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father, he will testify on my behalf.
Jesus sends the Spirit “from the Father”: the Son and the Father act together in the sending, and the Spirit's whole work is to point to Jesus.
You also are to testify because you have been with me from the beginning.

There is one testimony in two voices, the Spirit within and the Church without. Peter says the same before the council in Jerusalem: “we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit” (Acts 5:32).
ch: The Church hears in these verses her own mission. She is apostolic because she is built on the witness of the apostles and carries it on, guided by the Spirit (CCC 857). Pope St Paul VI wrote that people today listen more willingly to witnesses than to teachers, and if they do listen to teachers, it is because they are witnesses (Evangelii Nuntiandi 41).

qa: Did Paul think the law of Moses worthless, or the Jewish people rejected?

No. Paul speaks here as a Jew (2:15), and elsewhere he calls the law “holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). His argument is about how anyone, Jew or Gentile, is made right with God: by grace, through faith in Christ. Of his own people he writes that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29), and the Church teaches the same (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).
rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Mariam Thresia (1876–1926) of Puthenchira, foundress of the Congregation of the Holy Family. She went into the homes of the poor and the sick, cared for the dying and worked to bring peace to divided families. A daughter of the Syro-Malabar Church, she was canonised by Pope Francis on 13 October 2019, and her memory is kept with love by many in Kerala. Her life shows what Jesus meant by “you also are to testify”: a witness given less in words than in a whole life spent for others.
study: Paul would not let Christ's table have two classes of guests. Are there people I quietly keep at a distance in the Church?
The Spirit testifies, and so do we. Where is the Lord asking me to bear witness this week, and to whom?

lead: Today's readings set side by side the darkness that follows when God is pushed aside and the light that shines when he is met. Paul describes a humanity that “exchanged the truth about God for a lie” and was handed over to its own desires. At Bethany, near the tomb of Lazarus, Martha meets Jesus and hears, “I am the resurrection and the life.” Paul's picture of death is answered by Christ's word of life. The key words are exchange and believe.

r.h: They exchanged the truth about God for a lie
set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57–58, to a church he had not yet visited. After stating his theme, that the Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who has faith (1:16–17), he shows that all, Gentiles and Jews alike, need that salvation (1:18–3:20). He begins with the pagan world: God can be known through the things he has made (1:20), but people did not honour him as God (1:21) and exchanged his glory for images (1:23). Today's verses describe what follows.

The thought has a Jewish background, above all Wisdom 13–14, which says that the worship of idols is “the beginning and cause and end of every evil” (Wisdom 14:27). Then, in 2:1, Paul turns on the reader who has been nodding in agreement: “you have no excuse, whoever you are, when you judge others.”
str: vv. 24–25: God gave them up to impurity, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie.
vv. 26–27: God gave them up to degrading passions.
v. 28: God gave them up to a debased mind.
vv. 29–31: a long list of vices.
v. 32: knowing God's decree, they not only do these things but applaud others who do them.
kw: Three times (vv. 24, 26, 28). God does not push anyone into sin; he lets people have what they have chosen, and the choice becomes its own punishment. It is the same verb Paul uses of Christ, “handed over to death for our trespasses” (4:25), and of the Father who “gave him up for all of us” (8:32).

The key word of the passage: God's glory exchanged for images (v. 23, a related verb), the truth for a lie (v. 25), the natural for the unnatural (v. 26). Sin is shown as a bad bargain, a trading of the real for the false.
Against the order the Creator has placed in things. Paul's argument rests on Genesis 1: those who refuse to honour the Creator end by losing sight of the order of his creation.
vv: because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.
In the middle of the darkest passage Paul breaks into a blessing. A devout Jew could hardly name the Creator without blessing him.
And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind

There is a play on words in the Greek: they did not think it fit (edokimasan) to acknowledge God, so he gave them up to an unfit (adokimon) mind. When God is refused, even the power to judge rightly is damaged.
They know God’s decree, that those who practice such things deserve to die
The last stage is not weakness but approval: to call evil good. Isaiah had warned: “Ah, you who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20).
ch: The Church reads these verses as Paul meant them: as the first step of an argument that ends in mercy. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; they are now justified by his grace as a gift” (3:23–24). No reader stands outside the list of verses 29–31, which includes envy, gossip and boasting. From verses 26–27 the Church draws her teaching that homosexual acts are contrary to the natural law; in the same place she teaches that persons with such tendencies must be accepted with respect, compassion and sensitivity, and that every sign of unjust discrimination must be avoided (CCC 2357–2358). All are called to chastity, and all are offered the same mercy.

r.h: I am the resurrection and the life
set: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, has died. When Jesus heard of his illness he stayed two days longer where he was (11:6), saying that the illness was “for God’s glory” (11:4). Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives, about three kilometres from Jerusalem. The raising of Lazarus is the last and greatest of the signs in John's Gospel, and it leads directly to the decision to put Jesus to death (11:53).

Many had come to console the sisters, as Jewish custom asked of friends during the days of mourning. A later rabbinic tradition held that the soul stayed near the body for three days; whether or not that belief lies behind the “four days” here, John means that Lazarus is beyond all doubt dead.
str: vv. 17–19: Jesus arrives; Lazarus four days in the tomb; many come to console.
vv. 20–22: Martha goes out to meet him: sorrow and trust.
vv. 23–24: “Your brother will rise again”; Martha's faith in the last day.
vv. 25–26: “I am the resurrection and the life. Do you believe this?”
v. 27: Martha's confession.
kw: Martha uses the word of the general resurrection at the end of time, which many Jews of her day believed (Daniel 12:2; compare Acts 23:8). Jesus tells her that the resurrection is not only an event in the future: it is a person, standing before her.

One of the great “I am” sayings of John's Gospel: the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the way, the truth and the life. They echo the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14).
The question is put to Martha, and through her to every reader. John says he wrote his Gospel “so that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God” (20:31).
vv: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
Grief speaks honestly to Jesus. Mary will say the same words (11:32). Jesus does not rebuke the complaint.
I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live,
Bodily death remains, but it no longer has the last word. The life Jesus gives begins now, in faith and Baptism, and death does not break it.
Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.
Martha's confession is as full as Peter's in Matthew 16:16, and it uses the very titles of John's statement of purpose (20:31). She makes it before she has seen her brother raised.
ch: The Church hears in this Gospel her faith in the resurrection of the body: Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person (CCC 994). St Augustine, preaching on this passage, saw in Lazarus four days dead an image of the soul long bound by the habit of sin, whom the voice of Christ still calls out of the tomb (Tractates on John 49, in substance). Martha, often remembered only for being busy (Luke 10:40), is here the one who makes the great confession of faith.

qa: Why did Jesus wait two days before going to Bethany?

John gives the reason in Jesus' own words: the illness was “for God’s glory, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (11:4). He also says plainly that Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus (11:5). The delay was not indifference; it made room for a greater sign, through which many came to believe (11:45). God's delays in our own lives can also hide a larger mercy.
study: Paul says that sin begins with exchanging the truth about God for a lie. What false “gods” compete for the first place in my life?
Jesus asks Martha, “Do you believe this?” How would I answer him at the grave of someone I love?

lead: Today a little-known name meets one of the greatest promises of the Gospel. Paul sends home Epaphroditus, who nearly died in his service, and tells the Philippians to “honor such people”. In the Gospel Jesus promises that the Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all the truth. The Spirit's work is seen not only in great teaching but also in the quiet courage of people like Epaphroditus. The key words are service and truth.

r.h: Honor such people
set: Paul writes to the church at Philippi from prison (1:7, 13); scholars discuss whether he was held in Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea. The Philippians had sent Epaphroditus to him with a gift (4:18) and to stay and help him. In Paul's service he fell gravely ill. Now recovered, he is being sent home, probably carrying this letter. Just before, Paul has spoken of sending Timothy (2:19–24). Both men are living examples of the mind of Christ that Paul has just described in the great hymn of 2:5–11.
str: v. 25: who Epaphroditus is: brother, co-worker, fellow soldier, messenger and minister.
vv. 26–27: his longing for home, his illness and God's mercy.
v. 28: why Paul sends him back.
vv. 29–30: welcome him with joy and honour such people.
kw: The word from which “apostle” comes. Here it has its plain sense: one sent, the delegate of the church at Philippi. Paul gives this ordinary helper a title of honour.

A word for public service, used in the Greek Old Testament for priestly service in the Temple; from it comes “liturgy”. Paul uses the same family of words for the Philippians' help in 2:30 (“services”) and calls their gift “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (4:18).
A rare word for staking everything, as a gambler stakes his money. Epaphroditus put his life on the table for the work of Christ.
vv: He was indeed so ill that he nearly died. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, so that I would not have one sorrow after another.
Paul, through whom God worked healings (Acts 19:11–12), did not heal his friend at will. He calls the recovery mercy, for both of them. An apostle grieves and is relieved like any friend.
Welcome him then in the Lord with all joy, and honor such people,
Paul is perhaps forestalling any thought that Epaphroditus had come home early or failed in his task. He asks the church to receive him as a hero, not as one who fell short.
because he came close to death for the work of Christ,
The “work of Christ” here is very concrete: carrying a gift and caring for a prisoner. To serve a brother in need is to serve Christ: “I was in prison and you visited me” (Matthew 25:36).
ch: The Church sees in Epaphroditus the many who serve without becoming famous: those who carry help to prisoners, who nurse the sick, who keep a parish going. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Christian vocation is by its very nature a vocation to the apostolate, so that every member of the Church shares in her mission (Apostolicam Actuositatem 2). The passage also shows how the Church prays for the sick: with honest anxiety, with hope, and with thanksgiving when God shows mercy.

r.h: He will guide you into all the truth
set: Still in the farewell discourse. Jesus has said that it is to the disciples' advantage that he goes away, for otherwise the Advocate will not come to them (16:7), and that the Spirit will prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment (16:8–11). Now comes the last of the five sayings about the Advocate in these chapters (14:16–17; 14:26; 15:26; 16:7–11; 16:12–15).
str: v. 12: many things still to say, but they cannot bear them now.
v. 13: the Spirit of truth will guide them into all the truth, speaking only what he hears.
v. 14: he will glorify Jesus, taking what is his and declaring it.
v. 15: all that the Father has belongs to the Son.
kw: To carry a load. Before the cross and the Resurrection the disciples are not yet able to carry what Jesus has to tell them. Understanding grows as God gives it.

To lead along the way, as a guide leads travellers. The Greek Bible uses the same verb in Psalm 25:5: “Lead me in your truth.” The Spirit does not lead to new truths beside Christ, but further into the truth that Christ is (14:6).
To announce, to report. The Spirit passes on what he receives; he does not speak on his own. The word occurs three times in three verses (vv. 13, 14, 15).
vv: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.
God teaches as a good teacher does, at the pace of the learner.
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth;
“All the truth”, not “all truths”: the whole truth of Christ, unfolded over the ages.
All that the Father has is mine.
A plain statement of the unity of the Father and the Son. The Fathers used verses like this against those who denied that the Son is equal to the Father.
ch: The Church sees here how the one Revelation given in Christ is understood ever more deeply under the Spirit's guidance. There will be no new public revelation before the Lord's return (CCC 66), yet “there is a growth in the understanding of the realities and the words which have been handed down” (Dei Verbum 8; CCC 94). St Gregory of Nazianzus, explaining why the divinity of the Spirit was made plain only step by step, quoted this verse: the Old Testament proclaimed the Father openly and the Son more obscurely, the New manifested the Son and suggested the Spirit, and now the Spirit dwells among us and gives a clearer showing of himself (Oration 31, in substance).

qa: Why did Paul not simply heal Epaphroditus?

Healing is God's gift, not something an apostle commands at will. Paul also left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20), and he himself carried a “thorn” that God did not remove (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Illness is not a sign of weak faith. Paul prays, hopes and gives thanks, and he sees God's mercy in the recovery when it comes.
study: Who are the people like Epaphroditus in my parish, serving quietly? How can I “honor such people” this week?
Jesus says, “you cannot bear them now.” Which truth of faith have I come to understand only slowly, and how did the Spirit lead me to it?

lead: Today the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church keeps the Foundation Day of its hierarchy and remembers two apostles, Mar Barthulmai (St Bartholomew) and Mar Barnabas. The readings speak of a home given by grace. Paul says that through Christ “we have obtained access to this grace in which we stand”, at peace with God, with his love poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit. In the Gospel Jesus promises: “we will come to them and make our home with them.” The key words are access, love and home.

Paul speaks of what God has done: he has justified us and reconciled us to himself while we were still enemies. He also speaks of what follows: peace, and a hope that does not disappoint. Jesus speaks of the answer on our side: a love that keeps his word. Together the readings describe the Church as a household of God, received by grace, kept by love and filled with the Spirit.

r.h: God's love poured into our hearts
set: Romans 1–4 has shown that all have sinned and that God justifies by grace through faith, as he justified Abraham (ch. 4). Chapter 5 opens a new section of the letter: what life is like for those who have been justified. Paul begins with “Therefore”, gathering up all that went before, and the passage is full of “we”: Paul speaks as one of the believers, describing what all of them now share.

Two of Paul's words come from daily life. “Access” (prosagōgē) could describe being brought into the presence of a king, or drawing near to God in worship. “Reconciliation” (katallagē) belonged to diplomacy and family life: enemies, or estranged husband and wife, made one again. Paul uses both to say what Christ has done.
str: vv. 1–2: justified by faith: peace with God, access to grace, hope of glory.
vv. 3–5: boasting even in sufferings: endurance, character, hope; the love of God poured out through the Spirit.
vv. 6–8: Christ died for the ungodly: the proof of God's love.
vv. 9–10: “much more”: saved from wrath, saved by his life.
v. 11: boasting in God, through whom we have received reconciliation.
kw: Some ancient manuscripts read “let us have peace” (echōmen), others “we have peace” (echomen); the two forms differ by one vowel and sounded alike. Most modern translations, the NRSV among them, take “we have”; the Malayalam POC follows the reading “let us have peace”. Both say something true: peace is God's gift, and we are called to live in it.
Paul has excluded all boasting in ourselves (3:27). Now he names three right ways to boast: in the hope of sharing God's glory (v. 2), in sufferings (v. 3), and in God himself (v. 11).
The same verb root as in Joel's prophecy of the Spirit poured out on all flesh, which Peter proclaimed at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). The tense says the love was poured out once and remains.
God is the one who reconciles; we are the ones reconciled. The change is not in God's love, which came first (v. 8), but in our state: from enemies to friends.
vv: Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
Peace here is not first a feeling but a new relationship: the war between the sinner and God is over, and Christ has made the peace.
and hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.
St Augustine quoted this verse more than almost any other: the very love with which we love God is itself God's gift, poured out by the Spirit (On the Spirit and the Letter, in substance).
But God proves his love for us in that while we still were sinners Christ died for us.
God did not wait for us to become worthy. The love came first, and the Cross is its proof.
much more surely, having been reconciled, will we be saved by his life.
“Much more” is an argument from the harder to the easier: if God did the hardest thing for enemies, he will surely finish what he has begun in friends. “His life” is the life of the risen Christ.
ch: The Church sees in verse 5 the gift of the Holy Spirit as love itself: “God is Love and love is his first gift, containing all others” (CCC 733). Verse 8 stands at the heart of her teaching on the Cross: God's plan for us is one of love, prior to any merit on our part (CCC 604). The chain of verses 3–5 has long consoled those who suffer: trials borne with Christ become a school of hope. Hope here is not mere optimism; it is a theological virtue resting on God's faithfulness (CCC 1817–1818).

r.h: We will make our home with them
set: At the Last Supper Jesus has promised that he goes to prepare a place for the disciples in his Father's house (14:2–3). Now he turns the promise around: the Father and the Son will come and make their home with the one who loves him (14:23). The word for “dwelling places” in 14:2 and the word for “home” in 14:23 are the same Greek word, monē.

The question in verse 22 comes from “Judas (not Iscariot)”, called “Judas son of James” in Luke's lists of the Twelve (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13) and identified in tradition with Thaddeus. Many hoped that the Messiah would show himself openly to the whole world; Judas asks why the revelation will be to the disciples only.
str: vv. 15–17: love shown in keeping the commandments; another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, who abides with them.
vv. 18–20: “I will not leave you orphaned”: they will see him and live.
v. 21: the one who loves is loved and receives Christ's self-revelation.
vv. 22–24: Judas' question; the Father and the Son make their home with the one who loves.
kw: “Another” implies that Jesus himself has been their first Advocate (compare 1 John 2:1). The Spirit carries on his presence and his work.
A disciple without his teacher was like a child without a father. Jesus promises that they will not be left so.

From the verb menein, to abide, which runs through these chapters (15:4–10). God's dwelling with his people, once in the tent of meeting and the Temple, is now in the heart of the believer and in the Church.
vv: If you love me, you will keep my commandments.
Love is the root, obedience the fruit. Jesus does not say “keep my commandments and I will love you”, but the reverse.
I will not leave you orphaned; I am coming to you.
He comes at Easter, he comes in the Spirit, and he will come at the end. John holds the three comings together.
because I live, you also will live.
Our life hangs on his. Because the risen Christ lives, death cannot hold those who belong to him.
