Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.

This is the indwelling of the Holy Trinity in the soul of the just. The Catechism quotes this verse when it speaks of the final goal of God's whole plan: the entry of his creatures into the perfect unity of the Trinity, which begins even now (CCC 260).
ch: The Church reads this Gospel as the promise of God's indwelling: by grace the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit make their home in the baptised (CCC 260). The prayer of St Elizabeth of the Trinity, “O my God, Trinity whom I adore”, quoted in that same paragraph of the Catechism, is a prayer in the spirit of this verse. And the Church herself is the place where this home becomes visible: “a people made one with the unity of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit” (Lumen Gentium 4, quoting St Cyprian).

qa: Who was St Bartholomew, and is he the same as Nathanael?

Bartholomew appears in all four lists of the Twelve (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13). The name is Aramaic, Bar-Tolmai, “son of Tolmai”, which is why the Syriac Churches call him Mar Barthulmai. John's Gospel never names him, but it tells of Nathanael, brought to Jesus by Philip (John 1:45–49). Since the first three Gospels name Bartholomew next to Philip, many have identified the two, though this cannot be proved. Eusebius records an old report that Pantaenus of Alexandria found in “India” a Gospel of Matthew in Hebrew letters, left there by Bartholomew (Church History 5.10); which land was meant by “India” here is uncertain.
Was Barnabas an apostle?

He was not one of the Twelve, but Acts calls him and Paul “apostles” (Acts 14:14), and the Church honours him as an apostle. His name was Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, and the apostles called him Barnabas, “son of encouragement” (Acts 4:36). He sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet (4:37), stood by the newly converted Saul when others were afraid of him (9:27), and was sent to Antioch, where he is called “a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith” (11:24).
Does “justified by faith” mean that good works do not matter?

No. Paul says we are justified by faith, and in the same passage that God's love has been poured into our hearts (5:5). That love, given by grace, bears fruit in works. Jesus says the same from the other side: “Those who love me will keep my word” (John 14:23). Justification is the beginning of a new life in which, by grace, our good works become pleasing to God and merit eternal life (CCC 1987; 2008–2011).
rite: On 11 June 1932 Pope Pius XI, by the apostolic constitution Christo Pastorum Principi, erected the hierarchy of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church: the Archeparchy of Thiruvananthapuram under Archbishop Mar Ivanios and the Eparchy of Tiruvalla under Bishop Mar Theophilos. On 20 September 1930 the two bishops and their companions had entered full communion with the Bishop of Rome, keeping the West Syriac liturgy of their fathers. In 2005 the Church was raised to the rank of a Major Archiepiscopal Church. Today's readings fit the day: a people given “access to this grace in which we stand”, and a home where the Father and the Son make their dwelling. We thank God for the bishops, priests, religious and faithful of our Church, and we pray, with respect and love for our brothers and sisters of the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Churches, who share the same roots and the same liturgy, for the unity that Christ desires.

The two apostles remembered today link the day to the first preaching of the Gospel. Mar Barnabas was the bridge-builder of the early Church: he welcomed Saul when others held back, and at Antioch “when he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced” (Acts 11:23). That gift, to see grace at work and to rejoice in it, is one to ask for on this feast.
study: Paul says that suffering produces endurance, character and hope. Where have I seen that chain at work in my own life, or in the history of our Church?
“While we still were sinners Christ died for us.” How should this change the way I treat those I consider unworthy?
Jesus promises that the Father and he will make their home with those who love him. What kind of home does my heart offer them?
Barnabas was a “son of encouragement”. Whom can I encourage in faith this week?

lead: Two prayers stand at the heart of today's readings. Paul prays with all his heart for his own people, Israel, that they may be saved. A father kneels before Jesus and begs, “Lord, have mercy on my son.” Both readings ask what true faith is: not a righteousness of our own making, but trust in what God does in Christ, even if that trust is as small as a mustard seed. The key words are righteousness and faith.

r.h: My heart's desire and prayer for them
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul's long reflection on his own people. He has said that he has “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” in his heart for them (9:2), and he has listed with pride what belongs to them: “the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises” (9:4). He will end this section with hope: “all Israel will be saved” (11:26), for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). Today's verses must be read within that whole.
str: v. 1: Paul's prayer for their salvation.
v. 2: a zeal for God, but not enlightened.
v. 3: seeking to establish their own righteousness, not submitting to God's.
v. 4: Christ, the end of the law, so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.
kw: Paul knows this zeal from inside. He was once “far more zealous for the traditions of my ancestors” (Galatians 1:14), and “as to zeal, a persecutor of the church” (Philippians 3:6). He does not mock it; he honours it, and grieves that it has missed its goal.
God's own saving justice, by which he makes sinners righteous as a gift. “Their own” righteousness is one that a person tries to establish by his own observance.

The word can mean an end as a stopping point and an end as a goal. Catholic interpreters generally stress the second: Christ is the goal toward which the law was leading, and in him it is fulfilled (compare Matthew 5:17: “I have come not to abolish but to fulfill”).
vv: Brothers and sisters, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.
The first word Paul says about his people here is a prayer. That remains the Christian way to speak of the Jewish people.
I can testify that they have a zeal for God, but it is not enlightened.
“Not enlightened” is literally “not according to knowledge” (ou kat' epignōsin). Paul speaks with respect: he bears witness to their zeal before he names what is lacking.
For Christ is the end of the law so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.
“Everyone”: Jew and Gentile alike. A few verses later Paul says, “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all” (10:12).
ch: The Church reads these verses with the whole of Romans 9–11. She teaches that the Jews remain most dear to God because of their fathers, for he does not repent of the gifts he makes or of the calls he issues (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839), and she prays for the Jewish people as “the first to hear the word of God” (CCC 839). The Catechism quotes verse 4 when it teaches that Christ is the end of the law, because he alone teaches and bestows the justice of God (CCC 1953). Paul's prayer in verse 1 remains a model for the Church: to speak of others first in prayer.

r.h: Faith the size of a mustard seed
set: This scene follows straight after the Transfiguration (17:1–8). Peter, James and John have seen Jesus in glory on the mountain; at its foot the other disciples have failed to heal a boy. Mark tells the same story at greater length (Mark 9:14–29), with the father's cry, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24).

Matthew's word for the boy's illness, selēniazetai, means literally “moon-struck”, because people linked such seizures to the moon; the NRSV renders it “epileptic”. The Gospel speaks both of an illness and of a demon (17:18), in the language of its time. The Church today carefully distinguishes illness, which is the concern of medicine, from the presence of the Evil One, before any exorcism is performed (CCC 1673).
str: vv. 14–16: the father kneels; the disciples could not cure his son.
v. 17: “You faithless and perverse generation … bring him here to me.”
v. 18: Jesus rebukes the demon; the boy is cured at once.
vv. 19–20: “Why could we not cast it out?” Faith the size of a mustard seed.

¶ Verse 21 (“But this kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting”) is missing from the oldest manuscripts and the NRSV gives it only in a footnote; it was probably added from Mark 9:29. The POC joins the end of verse 20 to the number 21.
kw: Matthew's favourite reproach to the disciples: the noun here, and the related adjective oligopistoi, “you of little faith” (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8). It is not no faith, but weak and divided faith, faith that looks at the storm instead of at the Lord.
Proverbially the smallest of seeds (13:31–32). Jesus does not ask for great faith but for real faith: a small seed that is alive can move what seems immovable.

The words echo the Song of Moses about Israel in the wilderness, “a perverse and crooked generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5). The reproach falls on the whole generation, the disciples included, and not on the suffering father.
vv: Lord, have mercy on my son,
The father's prayer is the prayer of every parent, and it is close to the Church's oldest cry, Kyrie eleison, which the Holy Qurbono repeats many times.
Why could we not cast it out?
The disciples ask in private. It is a model for bringing our failures to the Lord honestly.
if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move;
“Moving mountains” was a proverbial image for doing what seems impossible. The mountain of the Transfiguration stands just behind them.
ch: The Church sees in this Gospel the power of faith joined to prayer. Mark's form of the saying, “This kind can come out only through prayer” (Mark 9:29), and the later reading that adds fasting, have shaped the Church's practice of meeting evil with prayer and fasting. For the Syro-Malankara faithful the Apostles' Fast begins on Wednesday 16 June: a time to bring the “mountains” of our lives to the Lord in that spirit. The father also teaches parents to bring their children to Christ in prayer, even when others have failed to help.

qa: Does Jesus mean that with enough faith we can get anything we want?

No. Faith is trust in God, not power over him. Jesus himself prayed, “yet not what I want but what you want” (Matthew 26:39). The promise that “nothing will be impossible” rests on God, of whom the angel said to Mary, “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). Mustard-seed faith places the mountain in God's hands and leaves the way it moves to him.
study: Paul's first words about those who had not accepted Christ are a prayer. How do I speak of people who do not share my faith?
What “mountain” in my life or my family seems immovable? How can I bring it to the Lord with mustard-seed faith, prayer and fasting, as the Apostles' Fast draws near?

lead: On this Fourth Sunday after Pentecost the readings speak of people whom God sends, blesses and keeps as his own. In the evening Gospel (Luke 10:1–16) the Lord sends seventy others ahead of him in pairs; before he tells them anything else, he tells them to pray: “ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.” Joshua 6:14–18 shows Israel circling Jericho until Joshua cries, “Shout! For the Lord has given you the city.” Psalm 15 asks, “O Lord, who may abide in your tent?” and answers with a portrait of the honest and upright person. In Isaiah 65:8–12 God compares his people to a cluster of grapes that is not destroyed, “for there is a blessing in it”. In Acts 6:1–7 the apostles ask the community to choose “seven men of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom” to serve at the tables.

We study three readings more closely. Deuteronomy 33 gives the last blessings of Moses and ends with a hymn: “Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the Lord”. Paul tells the Corinthians that the cup we bless and the bread we break are a true sharing in the blood and body of Christ, and so they cannot also sit at the table of idols. In the Gospel the seventy return full of joy because the demons submit to them, and Jesus turns their joy to its deepest ground: “rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The key words today are blessing, communion and belonging.

r.h: Happy are you, O Israel
set: Deuteronomy ends with the farewell of Moses. Before he climbs Mount Nebo to die (chapter 34), he blesses the tribes of Israel one by one, as Jacob had blessed his sons long before (Genesis 49). The blessing is an ancient poem. Many scholars think it is older than the book around it, and that it was placed here as Moses' last words. A short hymn to God opens it (33:2–5) and another closes it (33:26–29); the blessings of the tribes stand in between.

Our verses give the last two tribal blessings, for Naphtali and Asher, and then the closing hymn. Naphtali settled in the hills west of the Sea of Galilee; Asher along the coast to the north, in rich olive country. Centuries later Isaiah promised light to “the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali” (Isaiah 9:1), and Matthew sees that promise fulfilled when Jesus begins to preach in Galilee (Matthew 4:15).
str: v. 23: Naphtali, full of the Lord's favour and blessing.
vv. 24–25: Asher, blessed among his brothers, with oil in abundance and strength for all his days.
vv. 26–27: there is none like God, who rides the heavens to help his people and drives out their enemies.
vv. 28–29: Israel dwells in safety; “Happy are you, O Israel!”
¶ The tribal blessings end, and the whole people is gathered into one final word of praise for the God who saves them.
kw: In the Bible a blessing is not only a kind wish. It is God's gift of life, fruitfulness and peace, spoken over a person and believed to be effective. Moses blesses because he speaks for the Lord.
A rare poetic name for Israel, found only here, in 32:15 and 33:5, and in Isaiah 44:2. It probably comes from the root meaning “upright”: Israel as God calls it to be.
The same word opens the Psalter: “Happy are those who do not follow the advice of the wicked” (Psalm 1:1). It describes the person or people who are truly well off because they belong to God.
vv: O Naphtali, sated with favor, full of the blessing of the Lord,

The NRSV's “the west” renders the Hebrew word for “sea”, which here probably means the lake of Galilee. The POC keeps “sea”. Naphtali's land was the land where Jesus would later spend most of his public life.
There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to your help,
The picture of God riding the clouds is old Near Eastern language for the Lord of the storm and the sky. Israel uses it to say that the true God, and no other, is the one who comes to help.
he drove out the enemy before you, and said, “Destroy!”

The first half of this verse is hard in Hebrew. The NRSV adopts a corrected reading, “He subdues the ancient gods”. The traditional Hebrew text, which the POC follows, reads in substance: “The eternal God is your refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.” Both say that Israel's safety rests on God alone.
Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the Lord,

Israel's happiness is not its own strength but its Saviour. The verse ends with the enemy under Israel's feet. The Hebrew word there, bāmôt, can mean “backs” (NRSV) or “high places” (POC). The image of treading down the enemy returns in today's Gospel.
ch: The Church reads Moses' blessing as a witness to the faithfulness of God, who keeps the people he has chosen. St Paul says of Israel that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29), and the Catechism teaches that the Jewish people, “to whom the Lord our God spoke first”, keep a unique bond with the Church (CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4). Christians also hear in this blessing a promise that reaches beyond Israel: in Christ Jesus “the blessing of Abraham” comes to the nations (Galatians 3:14). So the Church does not take Israel's place. She is brought into a blessing that was first spoken over Israel, and she prays with Israel's own words: “Happy are you … a people saved by the Lord.”

r.h: One bread, one body
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (16:8), around AD 54–55. In chapters 8–10 he answers a real question of the Corinthian Christians: may they eat meat that has been offered to idols? In a city like Corinth, temples had dining rooms where sacrificial meals were held, and such meals were part of ordinary social life: family feasts, guild dinners, celebrations.

Paul first says that idols are nothing, and that the strong must take care not to wound the conscience of the weak (chapter 8). Then he warns from Israel's story in the desert: they all ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink, and yet many fell into idolatry (10:1–13). Our passage draws the conclusion. Eating at a temple feast is not a neutral act, because every sacred meal joins the eater to the one who is worshipped.
str: v. 14: flee from the worship of idols.
v. 15: Paul appeals to their own judgment.
vv. 16–17: the cup of blessing and the bread that we break: a sharing in the blood and body of Christ; one bread, one body.
v. 18: Israel's sacrifices make the eaters partners in the altar.
vv. 19–20: idols are nothing, but pagan sacrifice is turned away from God.
vv. 21–22: no one can share both the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
kw: The word means a real participation in something held in common. It is the word behind “Holy Communion”. Paul does not say the cup is a reminder of Christ's blood; he says it is a sharing in it.

In Jewish usage this is the name of the cup of wine over which the blessing of God is said at a festive meal; at the Passover meal it is the third cup. The Lord's Supper was celebrated in the setting of such a meal.
The prophet Malachi already speaks of the altar of the Temple as “the Lord's table” (Malachi 1:7). For Paul the table of the Lord is the altar of the new covenant.
vv: Therefore, my dear friends, flee from the worship of idols.
Paul does not say “argue about idols” but “flee”. Idolatry is not only bowing before statues. Anything that takes God's place in the heart can become an idol.
The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?

Paul names the cup first, perhaps because the cup was the point of comparison with pagan drink offerings. The question expects the answer “Yes”. The Corinthians already believe it; Paul builds his argument on what they believe.
Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
Here Paul moves from the body of Christ received to the body of Christ that we become. Communion with the Lord makes communion with one another.
You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
The word “cannot” is strong. It is not only forbidden; it is impossible, because the two tables lead in opposite directions.
ch: The Catechism explains the name “Holy Communion” from these verses: by this sacrament we unite ourselves to Christ, who makes us sharers in his Body and Blood to form a single body (CCC 1331). It also teaches that the Eucharist makes the Church: those who receive it are united more closely to Christ and so to one another (CCC 1396). The Second Vatican Council quotes verse 17 when it describes the Church as the Body of Christ (Lumen Gentium 7). St Augustine, preaching to the newly baptized on this mystery, told them that if they are the body of Christ and his members, it is their own mystery that is placed on the Lord's table: “be what you see, and receive what you are” (Sermon 272, in substance). For Paul's argument to hold, the sharing must be real: in the Holy Qurbono we truly receive the Body and Blood of the Lord.

r.h: Your names are written in heaven
set: Only Luke tells of this second mission. After sending the Twelve (9:1–6), Jesus sets his face towards Jerusalem (9:51) and appoints seventy others to go ahead of him into every town he means to visit (10:1). The evening Gospel gave his instructions; today's Gospel tells of their return.

The manuscripts are divided between “seventy” and “seventy-two” in 10:1 and 10:17. The NRSV reads “seventy”; the POC reads “seventy-two”. Both numbers recall the list of the nations in Genesis 10, which counts seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek Septuagint. The number seems to point beyond Israel to the whole world, which the Church will one day be sent to.
str: v. 17: the seventy return with joy: even the demons submit.
v. 18: Jesus saw Satan fall like lightning.
v. 19: authority over all the power of the enemy.
v. 20: the deeper joy: names written in heaven.
kw: A word of order and rank: the demons are put under. The disciples' power does not come from themselves but “in your name”.
Lightning falls suddenly and all at once, and everyone sees it. The fall of Satan is not slow and doubtful; it is sudden and public.

The Greek perfect tense means written and still standing written. The image of God's book of the living is old (Exodus 32:32; Daniel 12:1), and Paul uses it for his co-workers, “whose names are in the book of life” (Philippians 4:3).
vv: Lord, in your name even the demons submit to us!
The disciples had been told to heal the sick and announce the kingdom (10:9). They found that even the demons gave way. Their joy is real and Jesus does not rebuke it.
I watched Satan fall from heaven like a flash of lightning.

Jesus does not describe a battle long ago. In the mission of his poor messengers he sees Satan's power broken. Many Fathers linked this verse with Isaiah 14:12, “How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star”, and with Revelation 12:9.
See, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy; and nothing will hurt you.

The language echoes Psalm 91:13, “You will tread on the lion and the adder”, and Moses' blessing, “you shall tread on their backs” (Deuteronomy 33:29). The enemy now is not a human people but the power of evil.
but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.
Success in ministry can pass, and even great gifts can be lost. What lasts is that God knows us by name and has written us among his own. This is the joy that no failure can take away.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the coming of God's kingdom means the defeat of Satan's, and that the exorcisms of Jesus are signs of his victory over “the ruler of this world” (CCC 550). The Church continues that work in Christ's name, above all in Baptism, where the one to be baptized renounces Satan. The Catechism also teaches that God calls each one by name, and that the name received in Baptism is a name for eternity (CCC 2158–2159). The seventy are a picture of every missionary, catechist and parent who speaks of Christ: they may see wonderful fruit, but their deepest reason for joy is that they belong to God.

qa: Were there seventy disciples or seventy-two?

The ancient manuscripts of Luke are almost evenly divided, and scholars still do not agree. The NRSV reads “seventy”, the POC “seventy-two”. The meaning does not change: the number recalls the nations of the world in Genesis 10, and perhaps also the seventy elders who shared Moses' spirit (Numbers 11:16–25). The Church has honoured these unnamed disciples as “the Seventy” in her calendars.
Is the Holy Qurbono only a sign of our unity, as some say?

Paul's argument depends on more than a sign. He says the cup is a sharing in the blood of Christ and the bread a sharing in his body (10:16), and in the next chapter he warns that whoever eats or drinks unworthily “will be answerable for the body and blood of the Lord” (11:27). The Church believes that Christ is truly, really and substantially present under the forms of bread and wine (CCC 1374). Because he is truly there, the one bread makes us one body.
Jesus says “nothing will hurt you”. Does that mean believers will never suffer?

No. Luke himself tells how Stephen was stoned and James was killed (Acts 7; 12:2), and Jesus warns the seventy that they go “like lambs into the midst of wolves” (10:3). The promise is that no power of evil can separate those who belong to Christ from God. Paul says the same: neither death nor life nor any power “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39).
rite: In the West Syriac tradition the Sundays after Pentecost show the life of the Church that the Spirit has gathered and sent. Today that life has three marks: the blessing of God, the one bread of the Qurbono, and the joy of mission. Just before Communion in our Holy Qurbono the celebrant lifts up the Holy Mysteries and proclaims that the holy things are for the holy, and the people answer by confessing the one holy Father, the one holy Son and the one Holy Spirit. Holiness is not our own; we share it at the table of the Lord. This week the Apostles' Fast begins on Wednesday 16 June and is kept until the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June. The seventy of today's Gospel tell us what the fast is for: that labourers may be sent into the harvest, and that we who are sent may keep our joy where Jesus places it.
study: Moses blesses each tribe by name before he dies. Whom do I bless, in word and prayer, in my family and parish?
Paul says that the one bread makes us one body. How does receiving Holy Communion change the way I treat the people who stand beside me in church?
Is there any “idol”, anything that takes God's place in my heart, from which Paul would tell me to flee?
Where do I look for my joy in serving the Church: in results, or in the fact that God knows me by name?

lead: Today our calendar remembers the prophet Elisha, and the Gospel names him: in his time many in Israel had leprosy, “and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.” Jesus uses Elijah and Elisha to show that God's mercy has always reached beyond the expected boundaries. Paul, for his part, tells the baptized that sin no longer rules them: they are “not under law but under grace.” The key words are grace and mercy without borders.

r.h: Not under law but under grace
set: In Romans 6 Paul answers an objection: if grace abounds where sin abounded, should we go on sinning so that grace may abound all the more (6:1)? His answer is Baptism. We have been buried with Christ by baptism into death, so that we too might walk in newness of life (6:4). Today's verses draw the practical conclusion with a “therefore”: live now as people who have passed from death to life.
str: v. 12: do not let sin reign in your mortal bodies.
v. 13: do not hand your members over to sin; present yourselves and your members to God.
v. 14: sin will have no dominion, because you are under grace.
kw: Paul pictures sin as a king trying to win back a kingdom it has lost. In Baptism the reign of sin is broken, but the believer must refuse to let it return.
The word is often used of weapons. Our hands, eyes and tongue can serve as weapons for wickedness or for righteousness. The body is not the enemy; it is the place where the battle is won.
vv: Therefore, do not let sin exercise dominion in your mortal bodies, to make you obey their passions.
Paul does not say that the baptized will never feel the pull of sin. He says they must not obey it. The struggle remains, but its outcome has changed.
present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and present your members to God as instruments of righteousness.
“Present” is the language of offering. The Christian life is a daily self-offering, the whole person placed in God's hands.
For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
The law showed what is right but could not give the strength to do it. Grace is God's own life in us, and it gives what the law commanded.
ch: The Council of Trent taught, and the Catechism repeats, that after Baptism an inclination to sin called concupiscence remains, left for us to wrestle with; it cannot harm those who do not consent to it and who resist it manfully by the grace of Christ (CCC 1264). The Catechism also teaches that the grace of the Holy Spirit has the power to justify us, cleansing us from our sins and communicating the righteousness of God (CCC 1987–1988). Paul's command is therefore not a heavy burden added to grace. It is grace itself asking for our willing cooperation.

r.h: Naaman the Syrian
set: Jesus has returned to Galilee “filled with the power of the Spirit” (4:14), and in the synagogue at Nazareth he has read from Isaiah 61. He tells his own townspeople, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:21). At first they speak well of him; then they ask, “Is not this Joseph's son?” Jesus answers with a proverb, “no prophet is accepted in the prophet's hometown” (4:24), and then with two examples from Israel's own Scriptures.

The first example is Elijah, sent in a time of famine to a widow of Zarephath in the land of Sidon (1 Kings 17:8–16). The second is Elisha, who healed Naaman, the commander of the army of Aram, when he washed seven times in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:1–14). Both were foreigners; both received God's gift through a prophet of Israel.
str: vv. 25–26: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath.
v. 27: Elisha and Naaman the Syrian.
vv. 28–29: the synagogue's anger; they try to throw him from the hill.
v. 30: Jesus passes through the midst of them.
kw: 1 Kings 18:1 speaks of “the third year”. Luke here, and James 5:17, give three years and a half, a figure that seems to have become traditional. Half of seven, it was also a symbol of a time of trial.
Luke's word for the healing of leprosy. It means more than a cure of the skin: it restores the person to the community and to worship.
vv: yet Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon.
“Was sent” points to God as the one who sends. The prophet goes where God directs, and God directs him to a foreign widow.
There were also many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.

Naaman was a commander of a hostile army, and at first he was offended at being told simply to wash in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:11–12). Yet humility and obedience healed him. Jesus' hearers knew the story well; what stung was its point.
But he passed through the midst of them and went on his way.

Luke does not explain how. The hour of Jesus' death has not yet come, and it will be in Jerusalem, not on a hill at Nazareth. His “way” is the journey that Luke will follow to the cross and the resurrection.
ch: Luke's Gospel and its second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, show the good news going from Israel to the nations. Today's Gospel is a first sign of that movement, told not to reject Israel but to show the wideness of God's mercy, which Israel's own prophets already knew. St Ambrose, explaining the sacraments to the newly baptized, saw in Naaman's washing in the Jordan a figure of Baptism: it is not the water by itself that cleanses but the word of God and the grace of Christ (On the Mysteries, in substance). The anger at Nazareth belongs to one town and one moment; the Church never reads it as a judgment on the Jewish people, from whom Jesus came and among whom he preached (Nostra Aetate 4).

qa: Why were the people of Nazareth so angry?

They had heard of the wonders Jesus did at Capernaum and expected him to do the same for his own town (4:23). Instead he reminded them that God had once passed over many in Israel to help a foreign widow and a foreign general. It is a hard word for any community that thinks it has a special claim on God. Luke is not blaming a people; he is warning every hearer, Christians included, against thinking that grace is owed to us.
rite: Our Church keeps today the memory of Elisha the Prophet. He asked Elijah for “a double share of your spirit” (2 Kings 2:9), and his ministry was rich in signs of God's care: oil that did not fail for a poor widow, a child raised to life, a foreign commander healed in the Jordan. Scripture adds that a dead man came to life when his body touched Elisha's bones (2 Kings 13:21), and the Church has seen in this a sign that God honours the bodies of his saints. On his day we ask for the same humility that healed Naaman, and for the courage to bring God's mercy to those whom others pass by.
study: Paul tells me to present my members to God as instruments of righteousness. What will I do today with my hands, my eyes and my tongue?
Naaman almost refused healing because the remedy seemed too simple. Is there a simple means of grace, such as Confession or daily prayer, that I neglect?

lead: Today we remember the first church built in the name of the holy Mother of God, and the Gospel speaks of true worship: “the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.” Paul, writing to Corinth, tells each believer to remain with God in the condition in which God called them, since what counts is “obeying the commandments of God”. Both readings ask where God is truly found and served. The key words are calling and worship.

r.h: Remain with God where you were called
set: In chapter 7 Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him: “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote” (7:1). Some thought that becoming a Christian meant changing everything at once: leaving marriage, changing one's social state, undoing one's past. In the middle of his answers about marriage Paul gives a general rule and illustrates it with two examples: circumcision and slavery.
str: v. 17: the rule: live the life to which God called you.
vv. 18–19: circumcised or uncircumcised: what matters is keeping God's commandments.
vv. 20–23: slave or not: in the Lord the slave is the Lord's freed person, and every Christian belongs to Christ.
v. 24: remain with God in your calling.
kw: For Paul the “calling” is first God's call to faith and to belong to Christ. Our outward condition is the place where we answer that call; it is not the call itself.
“You were bought with a price” (7:23; also 6:20). The price is the blood of Christ. Those who have been bought by him cannot again sell themselves to any human master.
vv: let each of you lead the life that the Lord has assigned, to which God called you.
Paul says this is his rule “in all the churches”. Holiness does not wait for perfect circumstances; it begins where God finds us.
Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing; but obeying the commandments of God is everything.

A striking sentence from a Jew who had been circumcised on the eighth day (Philippians 3:5). Paul does not despise his heritage; he says that what saves is God's grace received in faith and lived in obedience.
Even if you can gain your freedom, make use of your present condition now more than ever.

The Greek of the second half is brief and can be read two ways: “make use of your present condition” (NRSV text) or “avail yourself of the opportunity” (NRSV note). The POC takes the second: if you can gain your freedom, use the chance. Either way, Paul does not praise slavery.
In whatever condition you were called, brothers and sisters, there remain with God.
The last words, “with God”, are the key. Whatever our state of life, the real question is whether we remain in his presence.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a teaching on vocation: every state of life, married or single, rich or poor, can become the place of holiness (Lumen Gentium 41). Paul's words about slaves are not a defence of slavery. In his letter to Philemon he asks a master to receive his slave back “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (Philemon 16), and the Church teaches plainly that enslaving human beings is a sin against their dignity (CCC 2414). Paul's point is that no human condition can stand between a person and the call of Christ.

r.h: In spirit and truth
set: Jesus is resting at Jacob's well near the Samaritan town of Sychar. He has asked a Samaritan woman for a drink, crossing two boundaries at once, since “Jews do not share things in common with Samaritans” (4:9). As the conversation deepens, she raises the old question that divided the two peoples: “Our ancestors worshiped on this mountain, but you say that the place where people must worship is in Jerusalem” (4:20).

The mountain is Gerizim. The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses and had built a temple on Gerizim, which was destroyed by the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus in the late second century BC. Jesus' answer moves the question from the place of worship to the person in whom God is worshipped.
str: v. 21: neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.
v. 22: salvation is from the Jews.
vv. 23–24: true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.
vv. 25–26: the woman speaks of the Messiah; Jesus says, “I am he.”
kw: The word first meant to bow down in reverence. It comes again and again in these verses: the whole conversation is about worship.
Not simply “sincerely” or “inwardly”. In John, the Spirit is the Holy Spirit whom Jesus will give, and the Truth is Jesus himself (14:6). True worship is worship in the Spirit, through Christ.

Literally “I am”. In John this phrase often recalls the name God revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14). Here it is the first time in the Gospel that Jesus openly says who he is, and he says it to a Samaritan woman.
vv: Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.
“Woman” is not a cold word in John; Jesus uses it also for his mother (2:4; 19:26). The “hour” in John is the hour of his death and glorification. From the cross a new worship will begin.
for salvation is from the Jews.
Jesus does not set aside Israel's faith; he affirms it. The Messiah comes from Israel, and the Church never forgets this root (CCC 528; Nostra Aetate 4).
But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth,
“And is now here”: because Jesus is present, the new worship has already begun. The Father himself “seeks” such worshippers; worship begins with God's desire for us.
I am he, the one who is speaking to you.
The woman had placed the Messiah in the future. Jesus places him in the present, in front of her. She will leave her water jar and become a witness to her town (4:28–29).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the worship “in Spirit and in truth” of the New Covenant is not tied exclusively to any one place, because the whole earth is sacred and entrusted to the children of men. Yet when believers gather, they are the living stones built into a spiritual house, and so, where religious liberty allows, Christians build churches as visible signs of the Church living in that place (CCC 1179–1180). Churches dedicated to the Mother of God belong to this picture. The Council of Ephesus in 431 confessed Mary as Theotokos, Mother of God, because the one she bore is truly God; a church in her name is a confession of faith in her Son.

qa: If true worship is “in spirit and truth”, do we still need church buildings?

Yes. Jesus does not abolish places of prayer; he himself went up to the Temple for the feasts. He says that worship is no longer bound to one mountain or one city, because it is offered in him and through the Spirit. A church is the house where the Church, the people of God, gathers for that worship, above all for the Holy Qurbono (CCC 1180–1181). The building serves the living temple; it does not replace it.
rite: Our calendar keeps today the memory of the founding of the first church in the name of the holy Mother of God. It does not say where or when that church was built, and we need not supply what it does not say. What it asks us to remember is that, very early, the disciples of Jesus gave houses of prayer the name of his Mother. In the Syriac tradition she is called Yoldath Aloho, the one who gave birth to God, and many of our parishes bear her name. Each such church is a sign that Christians come to the Son in the company of his Mother.
study: Paul tells me to remain with God in the condition in which I was called. Am I waiting for better circumstances before I try to be holy?
Jesus says the Father seeks true worshippers. How do I prepare to worship in spirit and truth when I come to the Holy Qurbono?

lead: The Apostles' Fast begins today, and the readings set the apostles before us. In the Gospel Jesus gives the Twelve authority and Matthew records their names, from “first, Simon, also known as Peter” to Judas Iscariot. Paul tells the Corinthians how to think of those who serve the Church: “as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries”, of whom one thing is required, that they be found trustworthy. The key words are authority and faithfulness.

r.h: Stewards of God's mysteries
set: The church at Corinth was divided into parties: “I belong to Paul,” “I belong to Apollos,” “I belong to Cephas” (1:12). In chapter 3 Paul answers that he and Apollos are only servants: one planted, the other watered, but God gave the growth (3:6). Chapter 4 opens with the conclusion: this is how you should regard us. Some at Corinth were also judging Paul and comparing him unfavourably with others; he answers that only the Lord can judge.
str: v. 1: servants of Christ, stewards of God's mysteries.
v. 2: what is required of stewards: trustworthiness.
vv. 3–4: Paul is not troubled by human judgment, nor does he judge himself; the Lord judges.
v. 5: wait for the Lord, who will bring hidden things to light.
kw: A helper who carries out another's orders. Luke uses the same word for John Mark, who assisted Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:5). The minister is never the owner of the work.
The manager of a household, often a trusted slave, who looked after the master's goods and gave each member of the household what was needed. He owned nothing; he answered for everything.
In Paul, God's plan, once hidden and now revealed in Christ (2:7). The Eastern Churches came to call the sacraments the Holy Mysteries, in Syriac rāzē, because in them that plan is given to us.
vv: Think of us in this way, as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries.
Two images: servants who obey, stewards who distribute. The ministers of the Church do not invent the faith or the sacraments; they hand on what they have received (11:23).
Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy.
Not brilliance, not popularity, but faithfulness. The same is asked of every Christian who has been given something to care for: a family, a gift, a task in the parish.
It is the Lord who judges me.
Paul's conscience is clear, but he knows that a clear conscience is not the final verdict. Only God sees the whole heart.
Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes,
This is not a ban on all judgment of right and wrong; Paul himself gives firm judgments in chapter 5. It forbids judging the hidden motives of others, which only the Lord can bring to light.
ch: The Catechism explains that the Greek word mystērion was rendered in Latin by two words, mysterium and sacramentum, so that the sacraments are the signs and instruments by which the one mystery of Christ is given to us (CCC 774). The Church has always applied this verse to bishops and priests, who are stewards of the Holy Mysteries, and it reminds them that faithfulness is what the Lord asks. It reminds the faithful, too, that they should pray for their pastors more than they judge them.

r.h: The names of the twelve apostles
set: Just before this passage Jesus sees the crowds “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” and tells his disciples to ask the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers (9:36–38). Now he himself sends labourers. Matthew 10 is the second of the five great discourses in his Gospel, the missionary discourse, and it begins by naming those who are sent.
str: v. 1: Jesus gives the Twelve authority over unclean spirits and every disease.
vv. 2–4: the names of the twelve apostles, in pairs.
kw: Not their own power but a share in the authority of Jesus himself, who has shown it over sickness, sin and the demons (chapters 8–9).
This is the only place where Matthew uses the word. An apostle is a messenger who carries the authority of the one who sends him.

Peter stands first in every list of the apostles in the New Testament, and Judas Iscariot is last in every Gospel list. Matthew adds the word “first”, which is not needed for counting; it marks Peter's place.
vv: Then Jesus summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to cure every disease and every sickness.
The words “every disease and every sickness” repeat what Matthew has said of Jesus himself (4:23; 9:35). The apostles are sent to do what Jesus does.
These are the names of the twelve apostles: first, Simon, also known as Peter,
Twelve recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus is gathering the people of God anew, and the Twelve are its foundation (Revelation 21:14).
Thomas and Matthew the tax collector;

Only Matthew's list adds “the tax collector” to his own name, remembering where the Lord found him (9:9). Thomas, named beside him, is the apostle whom the Christians of India have honoured as their father in faith.
Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, the one who betrayed him.

“Cananaean” is not about Canaan; it comes from an Aramaic word meaning “zealous”, and Luke calls him “the Zealot” (Luke 6:15). The list ends soberly with Judas: to be chosen is a gift that must be kept by faithfulness.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Lord Jesus gave his community a structure that will remain until the kingdom is fully achieved: he chose the Twelve with Peter as their head, and they are the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem (CCC 765). It also teaches that Simon Peter holds the first place in the college of the Twelve (CCC 552). The bishops are the successors of the apostles, and through them the authority given in today's Gospel continues in the Church.

qa: Why does the Church fast so soon after Pentecost?

Jesus said that his disciples would fast when the bridegroom was taken away from them (Matthew 9:15). After the Ascension and Pentecost the Church sets out on her mission, and in Acts the first Christians fast before sending out missionaries: “while they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul’” (Acts 13:2–3). St Leo the Great preached in Rome on a fast after Pentecost and spoke of it as handed down from the apostles (Sermons on the Pentecost fast, in substance). The Apostles' Fast is a fast for mission, kept in the company of the apostles.
rite: Today the Apostles' Fast, the Shleeha Nombu, begins in our Church, and it is kept until the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June. The fast is not only a discipline of food. It is a time to pray for the Church's mission and for those who carry it: the Holy Father, our bishops and priests, missionaries and catechists. Today's Gospel gives the fast its faces, the twelve names. It is good to pray for one apostle each day, and to remember especially St Thomas, through whose preaching, as our tradition holds, the faith first came to our land.
study: Paul says that stewards must be found trustworthy. What has God entrusted to me, and am I faithful in caring for it?
How will I keep the Apostles' Fast this year: what will I give up, and for whose mission will I pray?

lead: Both readings today are about foundations. Paul tells the Colossians to live “rooted and built up” in Christ, in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily”, and not to be carried off by teachings that do not come from him. Jesus ends the Sermon on the Plain with two houses: one built on rock by someone who hears his words and acts on them, the other built without a foundation. The key words are rooted and doing.

r.h: Rooted and built up in him
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. The church there was founded not by Paul but by his co-worker Epaphras (1:7). The letter warns against a teaching that called itself “philosophy” and mixed reverence for the “elemental spirits”, special festivals, food rules and the worship of angels (2:8, 16–18). Paul's answer is Christ: in him the Colossians already have everything.

The letter presents itself as written by Paul from prison. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in Paul's name, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.
str: vv. 6–7: continue to live in Christ, as you were taught.
v. 8: a warning against empty philosophy.
vv. 9–10: the fullness of God dwells in Christ, and you are filled in him.
vv. 11–12: the circumcision of Christ: buried and raised with him in Baptism.
vv. 13–15: God forgave us, cancelled the record against us, and triumphed over the powers.
kw: The phrase is debated. It can mean the basic elements of the world, or the first principles of a teaching, or spiritual powers thought to rule the world. In every case Paul's point is the same: nothing in creation can take the place of Christ.
God's whole being and life. It does not dwell in Christ partly or for a time, but “bodily”, really and permanently, in the Word made flesh.
A handwritten note of debt, signed by the debtor. Our sins had made us debtors before God; God has wiped out the bond and nailed it to the cross.
vv: As you therefore have received Christ Jesus the Lord, continue to live your lives in him,
“Received” is the word for receiving a tradition that is handed on. The Colossians did not receive only teaching about Christ; they received Christ himself.
For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
One of the clearest statements of the divinity of Christ in the New Testament. The Church has always read it with the faith of the Councils: Christ is true God and true man in one person.
when you were buried with him in baptism, you were also raised with him through faith in the power of God,
Baptism is not a symbol of something done elsewhere. In it the believer is joined to the death and resurrection of Christ.
erasing the record that stood against us with its legal demands. He set this aside, nailing it to the cross.
The picture is bold: the note of our debt is nailed up beside the Crucified, cancelled. What condemned us has been taken away.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Baptism signifies and brings about the Christian's descent into the tomb with Christ, dying to sin in order to walk in newness of life (CCC 628; Colossians 2:12). It also sees in the circumcision of Jesus a sign that prefigures the “circumcision of Christ”, which is Baptism (CCC 527). Paul's warning against empty philosophy does not condemn reason, which the Church honours; it warns against any system that would put something other than Christ at the centre.

r.h: The house built on rock
set: These verses close the Sermon on the Plain (6:20–49), Luke's shorter form of the teaching that Matthew gives as the Sermon on the Mount. Matthew's parable speaks of rock and sand (Matthew 7:24–27); Luke's builder digs deep to lay a foundation, and the danger is a river in flood. The image fits a land where dry stream beds can suddenly fill with water after heavy rain.
str: v. 46: the question: why call me “Lord” and not do what I say?
v. 47: the one who comes, hears and acts.
v. 48: like a man who dug deep and built on rock.
v. 49: the one who hears and does not act: a house without a foundation.
kw: The title of faith and worship. Jesus does not reject it; he asks that it be true in life as well as on the lips.
Solid bedrock under the soil. The rock is his word heard and done; behind it stands Jesus himself, the sure foundation.
vv: Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I tell you?
A gentle but searching question. Prayer and worship are not opposed to action; they are meant to lead into it.
That one is like a man building a house, who dug deeply and laid the foundation on rock;
Digging deeply takes time and effort and cannot be seen once the house stands. So it is with prayer, Scripture and the sacraments: the hidden work holds the visible life up.
But the one who hears and does not act is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation.
Both men heard the word. The difference is not knowledge but obedience. The storm does not create the difference; it reveals it.
ch: St James says the same: “be doers of the word, and not merely hearers who deceive themselves” (James 1:22). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the word of God is the support and energy of the Church, the food of the soul and the pure and lasting source of spiritual life (Dei Verbum 21). The house built on rock is the life that receives this word not only in the ear but in the hands.

qa: Does “nailing the record to the cross” mean that God's commandments no longer bind Christians?

No. What is nailed to the cross is the record of our debt, the sentence that stood against us, not God's holy will. Jesus himself said, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17), and the Church teaches that the Ten Commandments bind Christians (CCC 2068). Grace does not abolish the commandments; it gives us the strength to keep them out of love.
study: Paul says that in Christ I have come to fullness. Where am I looking for fullness elsewhere?
What is one word of Jesus that I have heard many times but have not yet put into practice?

lead: Today we keep the memory of Mar Aprem Malpan, St Ephrem the Syrian, the poet of our Syriac tradition, who loved to find Christ foreshadowed throughout the Scriptures. The Epistle fits him well: the law has “only a shadow of the good things to come”. In the Gospel Jesus shows us the reality behind every shadow: love that lays down its life for friends. “I have called you friends.” The key words are shadow and friendship.

r.h: A shadow of the good things to come
set: The Letter to the Hebrews does not name its author. Ancient tradition linked it with Paul, but already in the third century Origen said that only God knows who wrote it. It is a long sermon to Christians tempted to grow tired in faith, and its centre is Christ the high priest. In chapters 8–10 the author compares the sacrifices of the first covenant, above all those of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), with the one sacrifice of Christ. Our verses explain why the old sacrifices were repeated year after year.
str: v. 1: the law has a shadow, not the true form; its sacrifices cannot make perfect.
v. 2: if they could, they would have ceased.
v. 3: instead, they bring a yearly reminder of sin.
v. 4: the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins.
kw: A shadow shows the outline of something real but is not the thing itself. The eikōn is the reality in its own form. The worship of Israel was given by God and was true worship, but it pointed beyond itself to Christ.

The same word Jesus uses at the Last Supper: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). The old sacrifices recalled sin each year; the new remembrance makes present the sacrifice that takes sin away.
vv: Since the law has only a shadow of the good things to come and not the true form of these realities,
The “good things to come” have now come in Christ. The shadow is not despised; it is honoured as the sign that the light was coming.
But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sin year after year.
On the Day of Atonement the high priest entered the Holy of Holies once a year. The repetition itself showed that the final cleansing had not yet come.
For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

The psalms and the prophets had already said that God desires mercy and a contrite heart more than sacrifice (Psalm 51:16–17; Hosea 6:6). Hebrews goes on to quote Psalm 40: “a body you have prepared for me” (10:5). The true sacrifice is the self-offering of the Son.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the priesthood of the old covenant, though instituted by God, was powerless to bring about salvation, and so needed to repeat its sacrifices without end; only Christ's sacrifice, offered once for all, achieves it (CCC 1540). The Holy Qurbono does not add new sacrifices to his. It makes present the one sacrifice of the cross, so that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice (CCC 1366–1367). The shadows of Israel's worship are fulfilled, not erased.

r.h: I have called you friends
set: These words belong to the farewell discourse at the Last Supper. Jesus has just spoken of himself as the true vine and his disciples as the branches (15:1–8), and has told them, “As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love” (15:9). Now he explains what that love asks and gives: joy, the commandment of love, friendship, and lasting fruit.
str: v. 11: that my joy may be in you.
v. 12: the commandment: love one another as I have loved you.
v. 13: no greater love than to lay down one's life for friends.
vv. 14–15: you are my friends; I have made known everything.
vv. 16–17: I chose you to bear lasting fruit; love one another.
kw: In the Old Testament, Abraham is called God's friend (Isaiah 41:8), and the Lord spoke to Moses “face to face, as one speaks to a friend” (Exodus 33:11). Jesus now gives this title to all his disciples.
The self-giving love that seeks the good of the other. Its measure is not our feeling but “as I have loved you”: the love shown on the cross.
The key word of chapter 15. The branch remains in the vine, the disciple in Jesus' love, and the fruit lasts.
vv: This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
“As I have loved you” makes the commandment new (13:34). It is not only “as you love yourself” but as Christ loves: to the end.
No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.
Jesus speaks these words a few hours before he lays down his own life. The commandment is preceded and made possible by his example.
but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.
A servant receives orders; a friend receives confidences. Jesus shares with his disciples what is in the Father's heart.
You did not choose me but I chose you.
Every vocation begins with Christ's choice. In rabbinic custom a disciple chose his master; here the master chooses the disciples, and sends them to bear fruit.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus makes charity the new commandment, and that by loving his own to the end he shows the Father's love which he receives; by loving one another, the disciples imitate the love of Jesus which they themselves receive (CCC 1823). The friendship of which Jesus speaks is the heart of Christian prayer and life. It is offered to every disciple, and the saints are those who accepted it without reserve.

qa: Does Hebrews say that the sacrifices of the Old Testament were worthless?

No. They were given by God, offered in obedience and faith, and they taught Israel about sin, holiness and God's mercy. Hebrews says they were a shadow, which means they were real signs of a reality still to come. The Church honours them as part of God's plan and sees in them a preparation for Christ (CCC 1540). The one who fulfils them is himself a son of Israel.
rite: Our Church keeps today the memory of Mar Aprem Malpan, St Ephrem the Syrian. He was born at Nisibis in Mesopotamia early in the fourth century, served there as a deacon and teacher, and when Nisibis was handed over to Persia in 363 he moved with many Christians to Edessa, where he died in 373. He remained a deacon all his life. His hymns, the madrāšē, taught the faith in song, and the Syriac Churches still pray with them; tradition calls him the Harp of the Spirit. In 1920 Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church. Ephrem loved to see in Scripture and in nature symbols that point to Christ, and he would have recognized in today's Epistle his own way of reading: the shadows of the law are true, and they lead to the Son. He is a fitting patron for the Apostles' Fast, a man of prayer and fasting who, as tradition remembers, organised help for the hungry when famine struck Edessa.
study: Hebrews calls the old sacrifices a shadow of good things to come. How does knowing the Old Testament help me understand what happens in the Holy Qurbono?
Jesus calls me his friend. What would change in my prayer if I spoke to him as a friend who has chosen me?

lead: Both readings today are about a will joined to God's will. Hebrews lets us hear the Son say to the Father as he comes into the world: “See, God, I have come to do your will.” In Matthew, Jesus shows what that will looks like when someone wrongs us: no revenge, the second mile, and love even for the enemy. On this Saturday of the Apostles' Fast we also remember St Jude Thaddaeus, one of the Twelve. The key words are body, will and enemy.

r.h: See, I have come to do your will
set: The Letter to the Hebrews does not name its author. The early Church in the East received it among the letters of Paul; already in the third century Origen said that only God knows who wrote it. It is a long sermon to Christians who were tempted to grow tired and fall back. Chapters 8 to 10 compare the sacrifices of the old covenant, repeated year after year, with the one sacrifice of Christ.

Just before our passage the author says that “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (10:4). He then puts the words of Psalm 40 on the lips of Christ. He quotes the psalm in its Greek form, the Septuagint, which reads “a body you have prepared for me” where the Hebrew text has “you have given me an open ear”.
str: vv. 5–7: the Son's words as he enters the world: not sacrifices, but a body and an obedient will.
vv. 8–9: the author explains: the first order of sacrifice is taken away to establish the second.
v. 10: the result: we are made holy by the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
kw: The key to the passage. The Hebrew psalm speaks of an ear opened to obey; the Greek speaks of a body. Both point to the same thing: a whole human life given over to God. For Hebrews this body is the Incarnation itself, offered on the Cross.
God's will is not a cold decree. It is his saving plan. Christ's human will said yes to it at every moment, and in that yes we are made holy.
A favourite word of Hebrews (7:27; 9:12; 10:10). The sacrifice of Christ does not need to be repeated, because nothing is lacking to it.
vv: Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body you have prepared for me;
The prophets had already said that God wanted obedience more than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6). The old sacrifices were not bad, but they could only point beyond themselves.
See, God, I have come to do your will, O God
The whole life of Jesus is in this sentence. He says it at his coming into the world, in Nazareth, in Gethsemane (“not my will but yours be done”, Luke 22:42) and on the Cross.
He abolishes the first in order to establish the second.
The “first” is the system of animal sacrifices; the “second” is the doing of God's will by Christ. This is not contempt for Israel's worship, which God himself had given, but its fulfilment.
we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
“Have been sanctified” is a perfect tense in Greek: something done once whose effect remains. Holiness is first a gift received, before it is a task.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches the Incarnation: the Son took a body in order to offer it (CCC 462), and Christ's whole life is an offering to the Father, from his coming into the world to the Cross (CCC 606). The Church teaches that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Holy Qurbono are one single sacrifice: the victim is the same, only the manner of offering is different (CCC 1367). The Qurbono does not add a new sacrifice to the Cross. It makes the one offering present, so that we can join our own bodies and wills to it (Romans 12:1).

r.h: Love your enemies
set: These verses belong to the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5 to 7), and to a series of six sayings in which Jesus says: “You have heard that it was said… But I say to you” (5:21–48). He has just said that he came not to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfil them (5:17). These sayings do not cancel the Law. They go to its root, the heart.

“An eye for an eye” is found in the Law of Moses (Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21). It was a rule for judges, and it set a limit: the penalty must not be greater than the injury. In later Jewish practice it was generally applied as payment of damages. Jesus does not call the old rule cruel. He asks his disciples to go beyond justice to a generosity that breaks the chain of revenge.
str: v. 38: the old rule: an eye for an eye.
vv. 39–42: four examples: the cheek, the coat, the mile, the one who asks.
vv. 43–44: the old saying about neighbour and enemy, and the new command: love and pray.
kw: Here it means to strike back, to answer evil with evil, as in a lawsuit or a fight. Paul says the same: “Do not repay anyone evil for evil” (Romans 12:17).

A word from the Persian royal post. In Jesus' day a Roman soldier could make a civilian carry his load for a mile. The same verb is used of Simon of Cyrene, “compelled” to carry the cross (Matthew 27:32).
Not a feeling of liking, which cannot be commanded, but a will to do good to the other. Jesus joins it to prayer, the first good we can do for an enemy.
vv: But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also;

To strike the right cheek, a right-handed person would use the back of the hand. Many commentators think Jesus means an insult more than an assault. The disciple does not answer the insult with another.
and if anyone wants to sue you and take your coat, give your cloak as well;

The coat was the inner tunic; the cloak was the outer garment that also served as a blanket at night. The Law protected the poor man's cloak: it had to be returned before sunset (Exodus 22:26–27). Jesus asks the disciple to give up even what the Law allowed him to keep.
and if anyone forces you to go one mile, go also the second mile.
The first mile is forced; the second is a gift. The disciple turns an act of oppression into an act of service.
But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,

The Law of Moses never commands hatred of the enemy. It commands help even for an enemy's ox or donkey (Exodus 23:4–5), and Proverbs says, “If your enemies are hungry, give them bread to eat” (Proverbs 25:21). The saying “hate your enemy” in verse 43 was probably a popular narrowing of “neighbour”. Jesus opens the commandment to everyone.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in the Sermon on the Mount Jesus forbids anger, hatred and vengeance, and asks his disciples to turn the other cheek and love their enemies (CCC 2262). It also teaches that this does not take away the right and duty of legitimate defence, above all for those responsible for the lives of others (CCC 2263–2265). Jesus himself, struck before the high priest, asked calmly, “why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). What he forbids is revenge, not the defence of the innocent. Christian prayer reaches its height in forgiving enemies (CCC 2844).

qa: Does “do not resist an evildoer” mean that Christians must let evil go unchecked?

No. Jesus speaks of personal revenge, not of the protection of the weak or the work of just authority. Paul, in the same letter where he says “do not repay evil for evil”, says that rulers are God's servants for our good (Romans 13:4). The Catechism teaches that legitimate defence can be a grave duty for one responsible for others (CCC 2265). What the Gospel asks of each of us is to refuse hatred, to forgive, and to pray for those who wrong us.
rite: Today the Panchangam remembers Mar Yuda Thaddai Shleeha. Matthew and Mark call him Thaddaeus (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18); Luke calls him Judas son of James (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). John remembers one question he asked at the Last Supper: “Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?” (John 14:22). Old traditions tell of his preaching in the East and his martyrdom, though the details are uncertain. The short Letter of Jude bears the name of “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (Jude 1); whether this is the apostle is discussed among scholars. Jude learned the lesson of today's Gospel from the Lord himself: the love that prays even for those who persecute.
study: Hebrews puts Psalm 40 on the lips of Christ: “See, God, I have come to do your will.” Where in my day does God ask me to say the same words?
Who is the person I find hardest to pray for? What would the “second mile” look like with that person this week?

lead: On the Fifth Sunday after Pentecost, in the Apostles' Fast, the readings speak of what God gives to the weary and how he gives it through those he calls. The evening Gospel (Mark 9:30–37) finds the disciples arguing about who is the greatest, and Jesus answers: “Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.” Exodus 23:14–19 commands Israel to keep three pilgrim feasts a year and to bring the first fruits to the house of the Lord. In Zechariah 6:1–8 the prophet sees four chariots going out to patrol the earth. In Hosea 14:5–9 the Lord promises, “I will be like the dew to Israel.” In Acts 9:10–19 the Lord sends Ananias to Saul, “an instrument whom I have chosen”, and Saul is filled with the Holy Spirit and baptized.

We study three readings more closely. In Isaiah, God, who never grows weary, gives strength to those who wait for him. Paul tells the Corinthians that they are “the temple of the living God” and must live as God's own people. In Luke, Jesus feeds five thousand in a deserted place, but he does it through the hands of the Twelve: “You give them something to eat.” The key words are strength, temple and bread.

r.h: Those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength
set: Chapter 40 opens a new part of the book of Isaiah with the words “Comfort, O comfort my people” (40:1). Many scholars think chapters 40 to 55 come from a prophet of the time of the Babylonian exile, in the sixth century before Christ, who carried on the message of Isaiah of Jerusalem. The people had lost their land, their king and their Temple. Many felt that God had forgotten them.

Chapter 40 answers that fear by pointing to the greatness of the Creator. He measures the waters in the hollow of his hand (40:12); the nations are like a drop from a bucket (40:15); he calls the stars by name (40:26). Our verses draw the conclusion for a tired people: the God who made everything has not grown tired of them.
str: v. 27: Israel's complaint: “My way is hidden from the Lord.”
v. 28: the answer: the everlasting Creator does not faint or grow weary.
vv. 29–30: he gives power to the faint; even the young grow tired.
v. 31: those who wait for the Lord: wings like eagles, running, walking.
kw: those who wait for the Lord
The verb means to wait with hope, to look eagerly towards someone. It is not passive waiting but trust that holds on. The Greek Septuagint renders it “those who wait for God”.
Literally “shall exchange strength”. The image is of putting on new strength, as one changes a worn-out garment. God does not only add to our strength; he gives his own in exchange for our weakness.
In verse 27 it means one's case or right before a judge. The exiles felt that their cause had been dismissed. The prophet answers that the Lord still holds it.
vv: Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, “My way is hidden from the Lord, and my right is disregarded by my God”?
The prophet does not scold the complaint. He takes it seriously and answers it. Scripture is full of such honest prayers (Psalm 13:1: “How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?”).
He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable.
Human strength runs out; God's does not. His ways may be hidden from us, but we are never hidden from him.
He gives power to the faint, and strengthens the powerless.
The gift goes to those who have no strength left. This is the pattern of grace through all Scripture: “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint.
The order is surprising: flying, then running, then walking. The last may be the hardest: the long, ordinary road of each day, walked without giving up.
ch: The Church hears in these verses the virtue of hope, by which we trust in Christ's promises and rely not on our own strength but on the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1817). Hope keeps us from discouragement and sustains us in times of abandonment (CCC 1818). In today's Gospel the crowd that followed Jesus into the deserted place is tired and hungry, and he does not send them away. The God of Isaiah who gives power to the faint has come close in his Son, and he feeds us still in the Holy Qurbono, the bread for the journey.

r.h: We are the temple of the living God
set: Paul wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–57, to a church he loved but which had hurt him. Just before our passage he pleads: “open wide your hearts also” (6:13), and the same plea returns in 7:2. Our verses stand between them. Many scholars think this short section (6:14 to 7:1) may have been placed here from another letter of Paul, because its style is different, and the name “Beliar” occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Others see it as Paul's own sudden turn. Either way it belongs to the inspired letter as the Church received it.

Corinth was a great port city, full of temples. Christians were few, and much of social life, from trade guilds to family feasts, took place around the worship of idols. Paul had already said that believers do not need to leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:10), and that a Christian married to an unbeliever should not leave the marriage (1 Corinthians 7:12–14). Here he warns against partnerships that would draw believers back into idolatry.
str: v. 14a: the command: do not be mismatched with unbelievers.
vv. 14b–16a: five questions: righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness, Christ and Beliar, believer and unbeliever, God's temple and idols.
v. 16b: the reason: we are the temple of the living God.
vv. 17–18: a chain of Old Testament promises: come out, be separate, and I will be your father.
kw: Literally “yoked with a different kind”. It recalls the Law's rule not to plough with an ox and a donkey together (Deuteronomy 22:10). The two pull differently, and the furrow goes crooked.
A form of the Hebrew belîya‘al, “worthlessness”, used in Jewish writings of the time as a name for Satan. Paul sets Christ and Beliar as two masters who cannot share one servant.
The inner sanctuary, the dwelling place of God. Paul uses it of the whole community (1 Corinthians 3:16) and of each believer's body (1 Corinthians 6:19).
vv: Do not be mismatched with unbelievers.

Paul is not telling the Corinthians to despise their neighbours. He has just spoken of his own patience and kindness towards all (6:6). He warns against bonds that would make them share in idol worship.
For we are the temple of the living God;
In Jerusalem, God's presence was in the Temple. Now God dwells in a people. The quotation that follows joins Leviticus 26:11–12 and Ezekiel 37:27: “I will live in them and walk among them.”
Therefore come out from them, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean;
Isaiah 52:11 called the exiles to leave Babylon and come home pure. Paul applies it to the Christian's leaving behind of idolatry: a new exodus.
and I will be your father, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.
The words come from God's promise to David's son in 2 Samuel 7:14. Paul adds “and daughters” (compare Isaiah 43:6). The promise once made to the king is now made to every believer, man and woman.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Baptism makes the believer a temple of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1265), and the Second Vatican Council speaks of the Church as the temple built of living stones, in which God dwells (Lumen Gentium 6). The Church applies Paul's warning with care. She asks her children not to put their faith at risk, for example in marriage, and so she gives special attention to marriages between a Catholic and a person of another Christian Church or of another religion (CCC 1633–1637). At the same time she rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions and asks us to treat all people with respect (Nostra Aetate 2).

r.h: You give them something to eat
set: At the start of chapter 9 Jesus sent out the Twelve to proclaim the kingdom and to heal (9:1–6). Herod heard of it and asked, “who is this about whom I hear such things?” (9:9). Our passage begins with the return of the apostles, and soon after it Peter will answer Herod's question: “The Messiah of God” (9:20). The feeding of the five thousand stands between the question and the answer.

This is the only miracle of Jesus told in all four Gospels (Matthew 14:13–21; Mark 6:30–44; John 6:1–15). Luke places it near Bethsaida, a town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee. Readers who knew the Scriptures would remember the manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16) and the prophet Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, and some was left (2 Kings 4:42–44).
str: vv. 10–11: the apostles return; the crowds follow; Jesus welcomes them, teaches and heals.
v. 12: evening; the Twelve want to send the crowd away.
vv. 13–15: “You give them something to eat”; five loaves and two fish; the people seated in groups of fifty.
vv. 16–17: he blesses, breaks and gives; all are filled; twelve baskets left over.
kw: Literally “those who are sent”. Luke uses the title here, on their return from their first mission. The ones who were sent out now learn that they must also feed.

The Jewish blessing at meals praises God for the food: “Blessed are you, Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.” Jesus looks up to heaven and blesses God over the bread.
The Greek tense suggests action that goes on: he kept on giving. The bread did not run out while it passed from his hands through theirs.
vv: and he welcomed them, and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and healed those who needed to be cured.
Jesus had gone away to rest with the apostles, yet he welcomes the crowd. His first gift is the word, then healing, then bread.
But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.”
The “you” is emphatic in Greek. Jesus will do the miracle, but he wants the apostles to see the need as their own responsibility, and to bring what little they have.
And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, and blessed and broke them, and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.

Took, blessed, broke, gave: the same four actions return at the Last Supper (22:19, where Luke has “given thanks”) and at Emmaus (24:30). Luke's readers could not hear them without thinking of the Eucharist.
