And all ate and were filled. What was left over was gathered up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.
God's gift is not measured out sparingly. Twelve baskets, one for each apostle, and perhaps a sign of the twelve tribes: there is enough for all Israel and more.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord says the blessing, breaks and distributes the loaves through his disciples to feed the multitude, prefigures the superabundance of the unique bread of his Eucharist (CCC 1335). The Fathers saw in the apostles who carry the bread to the people a picture of the ministry of the Church. In the Holy Qurbono the priest does what the disciples did on the hillside: he receives from Christ's hands the bread that Christ has blessed, and gives it to the people. The miracle also speaks of charity: the Church cannot say to the hungry “send them away”.

qa: Was the feeding of the five thousand really a miracle, or did the crowd simply share the food they had hidden?

All four Gospels present it as a miracle worked by Jesus, a sign of who he is, and that is how the Church has always read it (CCC 547–549, 1335). The idea that the people merely shared their packed lunches is a modern guess with no support in the text. Sharing is a fine lesson, and it is in the story: the disciples give what they have. But the heart of the story is that Christ multiplies what is placed in his hands.
Does Paul's “do not be mismatched with unbelievers” forbid friendship or marriage with people of another faith?

Paul is warning against bonds that draw a believer into idol worship. He does not forbid ordinary friendship and work with others; he says Christians cannot leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:10). On marriage he says that a believer already married to an unbeliever should stay, because the unbelieving partner is made holy through the believer (1 Corinthians 7:12–14). The Church today allows marriages between a Catholic and a person of another Church or religion with the proper permission or dispensation and pastoral care, so that the faith of the Catholic partner and of the children is protected (CCC 1633–1637).
If God gives strength to those who wait for him, why do good people still grow tired?

Isaiah does not promise that we will never be tired. He says that “even youths will faint and be weary”. The promise is that God gives strength in our weakness, often enough for the next step rather than for the whole road at once. Jesus himself was tired and slept in the boat (Luke 8:23). Rest, prayer and the sacraments are the ways in which God renews our strength.
rite: This Sunday falls in the Apostles' Fast, which ends with the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June. The fast keeps the Church with the Shleehe, the apostles whom the Lord sent out to preach and to feed his people. Today's Gospel shows them learning that work: bringing their five loaves to the Lord and carrying his blessed bread to the crowd. In the West Syriac tradition the Sundays after Pentecost unfold the life of the Church that the Spirit has gathered, and this Sunday's readings, with Saul's calling in Acts and the servant-greatness of the evening Gospel, invite us to pray for those whom God calls to serve at his altar, and to give them our support.
study: Isaiah says those who wait for the Lord shall “walk and not faint”. What is the ordinary road I find hardest to keep walking, and how can I wait on the Lord in it?
Paul calls the community “the temple of the living God”. What in my home or parish honours that dwelling, and what dishonours it?
Jesus said to the apostles, “You give them something to eat.” What are my “five loaves”, and to whom is Christ asking me to give them?
How does the pattern “took, blessed, broke, gave” help me to understand what happens in the Holy Qurbono, and what it asks of me afterwards?

lead: Both readings ask the same question: whom do you serve? Paul tells the Romans that every life is given to some master, either to sin, which pays its wages in death, or to God, whose gift is eternal life. In Mark, the disciples have been arguing about who is the greatest, and Jesus puts a child in their midst. Yesterday's evening Gospel brought us to the same house in Capernaum. The key words are slave, servant and child.

r.h: Slaves of righteousness
set: Paul has just proclaimed that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (5:20). Some drew a wrong conclusion: then let us go on sinning. Paul answers it twice in chapter 6. The first time he speaks of Baptism, in which we died with Christ to sin (6:1–14). The second time, in our passage, he uses the picture of slavery, which everyone in Rome understood, since a large part of the city's people were slaves or freed slaves.
str: v. 15: the question: shall we sin because we are under grace?
vv. 16–18: everyone is the slave of the one he obeys; you have passed from sin to righteousness.
v. 19: present your members now to righteousness.
vv. 20–23: the fruit and end of each service: death or eternal life.
kw: Paul calls himself “a servant of Jesus Christ” (1:1), using this word. Belonging to God is not a lesser freedom. It is the only service that does not destroy the one who serves.
A soldier's pay, his daily ration money. Sin pays out regularly, and what it pays is death.
A gift of grace, given without being earned. Paul sets it against wages on purpose: death is earned, life is given.
vv: Should we sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means!
“By no means” is Paul's strongest denial, literally “may it not be!” Grace is not permission to sin. It is the power not to.
But thanks be to God that you, having once been slaves of sin, have become obedient from the heart to the form of teaching to which you were entrusted,

Paul does not say the teaching was entrusted to them, but that they were entrusted to the teaching, as one hands over a pupil to a master. The POC divides verses 17 and 18 differently, but the sense is the same.
I am speaking in human terms because of your natural limitations.
Paul knows that slavery is a poor picture of life with God, who calls us friends and children. He uses it because it makes the point clear: no one is without a master.
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
In the POC the first half of this verse closes verse 22. The contrast is complete: wages and gift, sin and God, death and life.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the more one does what is good, the more truly one becomes a person who can choose well: there is no true freedom except in the service of what is good and just, and the choice of evil leads to “the slavery of sin” (CCC 1733). It also teaches that death entered the world as a consequence of sin (CCC 1008), and that grace is the help God gives us, undeserved, to respond to his call to become his children and to share eternal life (CCC 1996). Life with God is called slavery only by comparison; in truth it is the life of sons and daughters.

r.h: Whoever wants to be first
set: Jesus has just told the disciples for the second time that he will be betrayed, killed and after three days rise again, but “they did not understand what he was saying and were afraid to ask him” (9:31–32). On the road behind him they talk of something else. In Capernaum, probably in the house of Peter (1:29), he asks them about it. Mark tells the scene in three short movements: a question, a saying, an action.
str: vv. 33–34: the question on arrival, and the disciples' silence.
v. 35: the saying: first by being last, great by being servant.
vv. 36–37: the child in his arms: welcoming the little one is welcoming Christ and the Father.
kw: One who waits at table. In 10:45 Jesus says that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. The Church's word “deacon” comes from it.
In that society a child had no rank and no rights. Jesus takes the one who counts for least and puts him at the centre.
To receive as a guest. To welcome a child “in my name” is to receive Christ himself.
vv: But they were silent, for on the way they had argued with one another who was the greatest.
Their silence is an answer. They knew their argument would not stand in the light of his question, and on the way to his Passion.
He sat down, called the twelve, and said to them,
A Jewish teacher sat to teach. Jesus gives this lesson with the weight of formal teaching, and to the Twelve, the future leaders of his Church.
“Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes not me but the one who sent me.”
The chain is the same as in Jesus' words when he sends out the Twelve (Matthew 10:40): the little one, Christ, the Father. Greatness is measured by how we receive those who cannot repay us.
ch: The Catechism teaches that to become a child in relation to God is the condition for entering the kingdom (CCC 526). The Church has tried to keep this saying before her pastors: from the time of St Gregory the Great the Bishop of Rome has called himself “servant of the servants of God”. Every authority in the Church is a service, and every Christian home that welcomes a child, the poor or the unwanted, welcomes Christ.

rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Aloysius Gonzaga (1568–1591). He was the eldest son of a noble Italian family, heir to a title, and he gave his inheritance to his younger brother to enter the Society of Jesus. In 1591, while plague struck Rome, he nursed the sick, caught the disease and died at the age of twenty-three. The Church has given him to young people as their patron. He chose to be last in order to serve, and in him the young can see that Paul's “slavery to God” is a life of joy.
study: Paul says that every person is the slave of the one he obeys. What do my choices of the last week show about whom I am serving?
Who is the “child” in my life, the person who cannot repay me, whom Jesus asks me to welcome in his name?

lead: Both readings are about where we put what we have. Paul asks the Corinthians to give generously to the poor of Jerusalem, because “God loves a cheerful giver” and will never let the generous be the poorer for it. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells us to store up treasure in heaven, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” In the Apostles' Fast, fasting and almsgiving go together. The key words are sowing, cheerful and treasure.

r.h: God loves a cheerful giver
set: Chapters 8 and 9 of 2 Corinthians are about the collection that Paul was gathering among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). At the meeting in Jerusalem, James, Cephas and John had asked him to “remember the poor”, which, he says, “was actually what I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10). For Paul the collection was more than relief. It was a sign that Jews and Gentiles were one Church. Some scholars think chapter 9 was first a separate note, perhaps to the churches of Achaia around Corinth; others read the two chapters as one appeal.
str: v. 6: the principle: sparing sowing, sparing harvest; generous sowing, generous harvest.
v. 7: give from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion.
vv. 8–9: God can give every grace in abundance, as the psalm says of the righteous.
vv. 10–11: the one who gives seed will multiply it, and the gift will become thanksgiving to God.
kw: The word that gives English “hilarious”, but here it means glad and willing. Verse 7 echoes the Greek text of Proverbs 22:8, which adds: “God blesses a cheerful and generous man.”
Having what one needs. The philosophers used it for being content with little. Paul uses it for having enough so that one can share abundantly.
In verse 6, “bountifully” is literally “with blessings”. A gift is a blessing to the one who receives it, and it calls down blessing on the one who gives.
vv: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.

Every farmer knows this. The seed thrown into the ground seems lost, but it is the only way to a harvest. Paul does not promise a financial return; the harvest he speaks of is the “harvest of your righteousness” (9:10).
Each of you must give as you have made up your mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
Paul will not force the Corinthians, though he has urged them strongly. A gift taken by pressure is not a gift. God looks at the heart of the giver more than at the size of the gift (Mark 12:41–44).
He scatters abroad, he gives to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.
From Psalm 112:9, which describes the righteous person who fears the Lord. Generosity to the poor is part of what Scripture calls righteousness.
You will be enriched in every way for your great generosity, which will produce thanksgiving to God through us;
The gift does not end with the poor who receive it. It turns into prayer: those who are helped give thanks to God. Almsgiving becomes worship.
ch: The Catechism recalls that from the very beginning Christians brought to the Eucharist, together with the bread and wine, gifts to share with those in need, and that this custom of the collection is inspired by the example of Christ, who became poor to make us rich (CCC 1351; 2 Corinthians 8:9). It also teaches that giving alms to the poor is a witness to fraternal charity and a work of justice pleasing to God (CCC 2462). In the Syriac tradition, as in the whole Church, fasting has always gone with almsgiving: what we deny ourselves is given to those who have less.

r.h: Where your treasure is
set: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus has just spoken of almsgiving, prayer and fasting, done in secret for the Father who sees in secret (6:1–18). Now he turns to possessions. Our three verses begin a short section that goes on with the eye as the lamp of the body (6:22–23) and the saying that no one can serve two masters, God and wealth (6:24). The thought was familiar to devout Jews: Sirach had said, “Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High” (Sirach 29:11), and Tobit taught that almsgiving lays up a good treasure (Tobit 4:9).
str: v. 19: do not store up treasures on earth, where they are lost.
v. 20: store up treasures in heaven, where they are safe.
v. 21: the reason: the heart follows the treasure.
kw: To heap up, to hoard. The noun is thēsauros, treasure or storehouse. Jesus does not condemn work or saving for one's family. He warns against making wealth the goal of life.
In the ancient world wealth was often kept in fine clothes, which moths eat, and in grain or metal, which decay. Brōsis means literally “eating”, anything that consumes.
In the Bible the heart is not only the feelings. It is the centre of the person, where we think, decide and love.
vv: where moth and rust consume and where thieves break in and steal;
“Break in” is literally “dig through”: houses were often built of mud brick, and a thief could dig through the wall. No earthly treasure is safe.
but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven,

Treasure in heaven is laid up by what we give and do for God and for others, above all for the poor. Jesus says to the rich young man: “sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (19:21).
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
Jesus does not say “where your heart is, there your treasure will be”, but the other way round. What we give our time and money to slowly shapes what we love.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse in teaching on the tenth commandment and the poverty of heart that Jesus asks of all his disciples (CCC 2544, 2551). Detachment from riches is necessary for entering the kingdom of heaven. St Augustine, preaching on this verse, calls the poor the porters who carry our goods ahead of us into heaven (Sermons, in substance). During the Apostles' Fast the Church invites us to look at our purse as well as our plate.

study: Paul says, “God loves a cheerful giver.” Do I give to God and to the poor gladly, grudgingly, or only when I am pressed?
If someone looked at how I spend my time and money, where would they say my treasure is?

lead: The epistle is the quiet ending of a great letter: Paul sends Tychicus to bring news and comfort, and closes with peace, love, faith and grace. The Gospel is the ending of a great sign: the man born blind, now healed and driven out, meets Jesus again and says, “Lord, I believe.” Some who claim to see remain blind. Both readings end in faith and love for the Lord. The key words are encourage, believe and see.

r.h: To encourage your hearts
set: Ephesians presents itself as written by Paul from prison (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). Many scholars think it was written after his death by a disciple who wrote in his name, because its style and some of its ideas differ from the letters that all agree are his; others hold that Paul wrote it himself, perhaps with the help of a secretary. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case. The words “in Ephesus” in 1:1 are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts, and the letter has few personal greetings, so it may have been meant for several churches of the province of Asia.

Our verses are almost word for word the same as Colossians 4:7–8, where Tychicus is also sent. Tychicus came from Asia (Acts 20:4) and was one of those who travelled with Paul on his last journey towards Jerusalem; later letters show Paul sending him on other errands (2 Timothy 4:12; Titus 3:12).
str: vv. 21–22: Tychicus is sent to bring news and to encourage.
v. 23: the blessing of peace, and love with faith, from the Father and the Son.
v. 24: grace to all who love the Lord Jesus Christ.
kw: Tychicus is a “faithful minister in the Lord”. The word does not yet mean the ordained deacon; it describes a trusted servant of the Gospel.
The verb can mean to comfort, to exhort and to strengthen. It is related to the name of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete (John 14:16).
The last word of the letter. The NRSV takes it with love: “an undying love”. It can also be read with grace, as a promise of immortal life. The POC follows that reading: “grace and eternal life”.
vv: Tychicus will tell you everything. He is a dear brother and a faithful minister in the Lord.
The letter has spoken of the vast plan of God to unite all things in Christ (1:10). It ends with a man on the road carrying news. God's great plan moves forward through faithful messengers.
I am sending him to you for this very purpose, to let you know how we are, and to encourage your hearts.
Paul is in chains, yet his concern is for their hearts, not his own comfort.
Peace be to the whole community, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
The Greek says “to the brothers”, which the NRSV renders “the whole community”; the POC keeps “brothers”. Peace, love and faith come from the Father and the Son together.
Grace be with all who have an undying love for our Lord Jesus Christ.
The letter ends where Christian life begins and ends: love for the Lord Jesus.
ch: The greetings of Paul's letters passed into the Church's worship. In the Holy Qurbono the celebrant again and again turns to the people with the blessing of peace, and the people answer, so that the liturgy itself becomes a letter of encouragement from Christ to his Church. Tychicus also reminds us that the Church has always needed faithful messengers: those who carry news, comfort the anxious and bind communities together. Every catechist and every visitor of the sick does the work of Tychicus.

r.h: Lord, I believe
set: Chapter 9 tells how Jesus healed a man blind from birth. He made mud, spread it on the man's eyes and sent him to wash in the pool of Siloam, a name John explains as “Sent” (9:7). Then the healed man is questioned by his neighbours, by some of the Pharisees and by his parents, and he is finally driven out (9:34). Throughout the chapter he sees more and more clearly: first “the man called Jesus” (9:11), then “a prophet” (9:17), then one who must be “from God” (9:33). In our verses he comes to full faith.

When John speaks of the man's opponents, he means some of the religious leaders of that time, not the Jewish people as a whole; even the Pharisees were divided about Jesus (9:16). Many scholars think that John's account also reflects later conflicts between the first Christians and the synagogue. The Church firmly rejects any use of such passages to blame the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4).
str: v. 35: Jesus seeks out the man who was driven out.
vv. 36–38: the dialogue, ending in faith and worship.
v. 39: Jesus' saying about judgment: the blind see, the seeing become blind.
vv. 40–41: the question of some Pharisees, and Jesus' reply.
kw: The oldest manuscripts read “Son of Man”; later ones have “Son of God”. Jesus uses the title of himself, as the one who comes from heaven and will judge (5:27).
To bow down before someone. In John this verb is used for the worship of God (4:20–24). The man born blind does not only thank his healer. He worships him.
The coming of the light divides. Jesus did not come to condemn (3:17), but his presence shows what is in each heart.
vv: Jesus heard that they had driven him out, and when he found him, he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”
The man was put out of the community, and Jesus goes looking for him. The Good Shepherd, of whom the next chapter speaks, seeks the sheep that has been cast out.
He said, “Lord, I believe.” And he worshiped him.
“Sir” in verse 36 becomes “Lord” here: the same Greek word, kyrie, now said with full faith. The healing of his eyes is complete when he sees who Jesus is.
I came into this world for judgment so that those who do not see may see, and those who do see may become blind.
Jesus speaks of spiritual sight. Those who know their blindness can be healed; those who think they see everything close themselves to the light.
If you were blind, you would not have sin. But now that you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains.
Not knowing can excuse; refusing to see cannot. The danger is not weakness but the pride that will not admit any need of healing.
ch: From early times the Church read this chapter in the preparation of those about to be baptized. St Justin Martyr already calls Baptism “enlightenment”, because those who receive it are enlightened in mind (CCC 1216). St Augustine saw in the man born blind the whole human race, blind from its first parents, anointed by Christ and washed in the waters of the One who was “Sent” (Tractates on the Gospel of John 44, in substance). The confession “Lord, I believe” is the answer that every baptized person is called to make, again and again.

qa: Does Jesus mean that the Pharisees were worse sinners than everyone else?

No. Jesus speaks to some Pharisees who were present and who refused to see. The warning is for every believer and every religious person, including Christians: the moment we say “We see” and admit no need of the light, our sin remains. Elsewhere John tells of Pharisees who came to faith, such as Nicodemus (3:1; 19:39).
study: Paul sent Tychicus “to encourage your hearts”. Whom could I encourage this week by a visit, a call or a message?
The man born blind came to faith step by step. Where am I on that road, and what would it mean for me to say today, “Lord, I believe”?

lead: Today the Church keeps the birth of Yohannan Mamdana, John the Baptist. The Gospel tells of his birth and naming: “His name is John”, and with those words his father's tongue is set loose to praise God. The epistle from Hebrews may seem at first a surprising choice, but it describes the life John would live: “Pursue peace with everyone, and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.” John lived that holiness in the desert, and he was the one who saw the Lord and pointed him out to others. The Panchangam also keeps today the memory of Cheppattu Philipose Ramban, a monk-priest, with its own readings: Hebrews 13:7–16, “Remember your leaders… and imitate their faith”, and Matthew 24:45–51, the faithful and wise servant whom the master finds at work.
We study the two readings of the feast. The key words are holiness, grace and name.

r.h: The holiness without which no one will see the Lord
set: The Letter to the Hebrews does not name its author; the Church has long read it with the letters of Paul. Chapter 12 opens with the image of a race: “let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus” (12:1–2). The author then speaks of hardship as the discipline of a loving Father (12:5–11) and urges the tired to “lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees” (12:12).

Our verses turn from encouragement to warning. Right after them comes the great contrast between Mount Sinai, with its fire and trembling, and Mount Zion, “the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (12:18–24). The warning is given to people who are on their way to that city, so that none of them should fall out on the road.
str: v. 14: the double command: peace with all, and holiness.
v. 15: watch over one another: that no one misses grace, that no bitter root springs up.
vv. 16–17: the example of Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.
kw: A strong verb: to run after, to chase. Peace and holiness do not happen by themselves; they must be pursued with effort, like the runner in 12:1.
The process of being made holy, a life set apart for God. It is God's gift (10:10), and it grows as we cooperate with him.
Literally “watching over”, the root of the word episkopos, bishop or overseer. Here the whole community is told to keep watch over one another.
vv: Pursue peace with everyone, and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.
To “see the Lord” is the final goal of the Christian life. Jesus says the same in the Beatitudes: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8).
that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and through it many become defiled.
The image comes from Deuteronomy 29:18, where it describes a person who turns away from God and poisons others. Bitterness hidden in one heart can spread through a whole community.
See to it that no one becomes like Esau, an immoral and godless person, who sold his birthright for a single meal.
The story is in Genesis 25:29–34. Esau traded what was holy and lasting for what was immediate. “Godless” translates bebēlos, one who treats holy things as common.
he found no chance to repent, even though he sought the blessing with tears.

The blessing had already been given to Jacob, and Isaac could not take it back (Genesis 27:30–40). Commentators differ on whose change of mind is meant, Esau's or his father's. The point is that some losses, once chosen, cannot be undone in this life.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that all the faithful, of whatever state or rank, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity (Lumen Gentium 40; CCC 2013). John the Baptist shows what that call can look like: a life stripped of everything that does not serve God, and a heart without envy, so that when people told him that everyone was going to Jesus, he answered, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). The warning about Esau does not close the door of mercy. The Church teaches that there is no offence, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive, if the sinner truly repents (CCC 982).

r.h: His name is John
set: Luke begins his Gospel with two births told side by side. The angel Gabriel announces the birth of John to Zechariah in the Temple (1:5–25), and then the birth of Jesus to Mary in Nazareth (1:26–38). The two mothers meet at the Visitation, and the unborn John leaps in Elizabeth's womb (1:39–45). Now the first promise is fulfilled. The birth of Jesus will be told in the same pattern: birth, rejoicing, circumcision on the eighth day, naming (2:1–21). John is always shown as great, but always as the one who goes before a greater.

When Zechariah doubted the angel's word, he was told he would be unable to speak until these things took place (1:20). Circumcision on the eighth day was commanded in the Law (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3), and by this time it was the custom to give the child his name at the circumcision.
str: vv. 57–58: the birth, and the joy of neighbours and relatives.
vv. 59–61: the eighth day: they want to name him Zechariah; Elizabeth says “John”.
vv. 62–64: Zechariah writes “His name is John”, and his mouth is opened.
vv. 65–66: fear and wonder through the hill country: “What then will this child become?”
kw: The Hebrew name means “The Lord has been gracious” or “the Lord has shown favour”. The name chosen by God sums up what is happening: God's mercy has come to an old couple and, through their child, to his people.

In verse 58 the neighbours hear that the Lord “had shown his great mercy” to Elizabeth. Mercy is the great word of Luke's first chapter: Mary sings of it (1:50, 54) and Zechariah will sing of it (1:72, 78).
A small wooden tablet, often coated with wax, on which one wrote with a pointed stylus. Zechariah's first words after months of silence are written: God's chosen name.
vv: Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown his great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
The angel had promised: “many will rejoice at his birth” (1:14). The promise begins to come true among the neighbours. Joy shared is a sign of God at work.
But his mother said, “No; he is to be called John.”

Luke does not say how Elizabeth knew the name. Many think Zechariah had written it for her; others see her speaking by the Holy Spirit, with whom she was filled at the Visitation (1:41). Either way, the family custom gives way to God's word.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And all of them were amazed.
Zechariah does not write “His name shall be John” but “His name is John”: the name has already been given by God. His obedience now undoes his earlier doubt.
Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue freed, and he began to speak, praising God.
His first words are praise. The words of his song, the Benedictus, follow in 1:68–79: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has looked favorably on his people.”
“What then will this child become?” For, indeed, the hand of the Lord was with him.

“The hand of the Lord” is an Old Testament way of speaking of God's power with his chosen ones, such as the prophets (Ezekiel 1:3). The question will be answered when John appears in the wilderness (3:1–6).
ch: The Catechism teaches that John is the Lord's immediate forerunner, sent to prepare his way; “prophet of the Most High”, he surpasses all the prophets and is the last of them (CCC 523). In John the Holy Spirit completes the work of preparing a people for the Lord (CCC 717–720). The Church keeps the birthday of very few saints, because she usually honours the day of their death. She keeps the birth of Christ, of his Mother, and of John. St Augustine noted in his sermons for this feast that in his day the Church kept the birthday of only two, the Lord and John (in substance). The feast falls six months before the Lord's birth, as Luke indicates (1:26, 36).

qa: Why does the Church keep John's birthday, when for other saints she keeps the day of their death?

Because John's birth was itself part of the good news. He was filled with the Holy Spirit even before his birth (Luke 1:15) and leapt for joy in his mother's womb at the presence of the Lord (1:41, 44). The Church therefore holds that he was already sanctified when he was born. That is why, besides the Lord's own birth, she keeps the births of only the Mother of God and of John the Baptist. His martyrdom is remembered too, on its own day.
Hebrews says that Esau “found no chance to repent”. Can a person ever be beyond forgiveness?

No one who truly repents is beyond God's mercy. The Church teaches that there is no sin so serious that it cannot be forgiven when the sinner turns back to God (CCC 982). Hebrews speaks of the blessing that Esau could not get back, not of God refusing a contrite heart. The warning is that we should not treat holy gifts lightly, as if we could always recover them later. The time to turn to God is now.
Was Zechariah deaf as well as mute?

Luke says that the people “began motioning to his father” (1:62), which suggests that he could not hear either. The word used for him in 1:22, kōphos, can mean both unable to speak and unable to hear. Luke wants us to see a man shut into silence until God's word is fulfilled, and then opened to praise.
rite: Our tradition names John Yohannan Mamdana, John the Baptizer. In the West Syriac calendar he already appears in the Sundays of Suboro before Yaldo, where the announcement to Zechariah and the birth of John are read on their own Sundays as the Church prepares for the Lord's birth. Today the Panchangam keeps the birth again in summer, in the Apostles' Fast. The memory of Cheppattu Philipose Ramban, kept on the same day, joins John's example with the call of Hebrews 13 to remember those who spoke the word of God to us and to imitate their faith. Like John, every faithful monk and priest is a voice that points beyond himself to Christ, the Lamb of God whom we receive in the Holy Qurbono.
study: Hebrews says, “Pursue peace with everyone.” With whom do I need to pursue peace actively, instead of waiting for it to happen?
Is there a “root of bitterness” in my heart or my family? What would it take to pull it out?
Elizabeth and Zechariah let God's name for their son replace the family custom. Where is God asking me to let his word come before what “everyone has always done”?
John's whole life was summed up in “He must increase, but I must decrease.” What would that mean in my work, my family and my parish this week?

lead: Both readings ask where true teaching and true faith come from. Hebrews looks back at the patriarchs, who trusted God's promise even when it seemed to lead to death: Abraham on the mountain with Isaac, Isaac and Jacob blessing sons they would not see grow old, Joseph speaking of an exodus that lay centuries ahead. In John, Jesus teaches in the temple at the feast of Booths and says that his teaching is not his own but the Father's, and that whoever is ready to do God's will shall recognise it. The key words are faith and right judgment.

r.h: By faith Abraham offered up Isaac
set: Hebrews 11 is the great roll of honour of faith. It opens with a definition: “faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (11:1), and then walks through the story of Israel, each example beginning with the same Greek word, pistei, “by faith”. Our verses come after the call of Abraham (11:8–16) and turn to the testing of his faith and to the blessings handed on by Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, all taken from Genesis 22 to 50.
str: vv. 17–19: Abraham offers Isaac, trusting that God can raise the dead.
v. 20: Isaac blesses Jacob and Esau.
v. 21: the dying Jacob blesses the sons of Joseph.
v. 22: the dying Joseph speaks of the exodus and gives orders about his bones.
kw: The word that begins each example of the chapter like a drum beat. Faith here is not a vague feeling. It is trust in God's word that shows itself in acts: leaving, offering, blessing, giving orders for a future one will not see.

The same word John uses of Christ, “the only Son” (John 3:16). Abraham had another son, Ishmael, but Isaac was the one son of the promise. The word prepares the Christian reader to see in Isaac a figure of the Father's only Son.
Literally “in a parable” or “as a figure”. Isaac did not die, but Abraham received him back as if from the dead, and this return was itself a sign pointing ahead.
vv: By faith Abraham, when put to the test, offered up Isaac.
The test of Genesis 22 seemed to set God's command against God's promise, since the promise was to come through Isaac. Abraham held on to both, trusting that God would not contradict himself.
He considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead
Hebrews reads the story of Moriah in the light of Easter. Abraham's faith reached beyond death long before the resurrection was revealed.
By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, “bowing in worship over the top of his staff.”

The phrase about the staff comes from the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 47:31. The Hebrew text has “the head of his bed”. The two words differ only in their vowels, which were not written in ancient Hebrew.
By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his burial.

Joseph asked that his bones be carried up from Egypt (Genesis 50:24–25). Moses did so at the exodus (Exodus 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). A dying man's faith looked some four hundred years ahead.
ch: The Catechism uses these verses when it speaks of Abraham's prayer and faith: asked to sacrifice the son God had given him, Abraham did not waver, for he considered that God was able to raise men even from the dead, and so the father of believers was conformed to the likeness of the Father who would not spare his own Son (CCC 2572). From the earliest centuries Christians have seen in Isaac, carrying the wood up the mountain, a figure of Christ carrying his cross, and in the ram offered in his place a sign of the Lamb whom God himself provides.

r.h: My teaching is not mine but his who sent me
set: Booths, or Tabernacles, was the joyful autumn pilgrimage feast, when people lived in shelters of branches to remember the wandering in the wilderness. Jesus had gone up to Jerusalem quietly, “not publicly but as it were in secret” (7:10). Now, half way through the week of the feast, he teaches openly in the temple.

The argument looks back to John 5, where Jesus healed a man at the pool of Bethesda on a sabbath and some of the authorities began to seek his death (5:16–18). In this Gospel “the Jews” often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus, not the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus, his mother and his disciples were all Jews, and “the crowd” in verse 20 does not know of any plot.
str: vv. 14–15: Jesus teaches; the hearers wonder at his learning.
vv. 16–18: his teaching comes from the one who sent him.
vv. 19–20: the law of Moses and the plot to kill him.
vv. 21–24: circumcision on the sabbath and the healing of a whole man: judge with right judgment.
kw: Literally “letters”. The question is how Jesus can teach the Scriptures so deeply when he has not studied under a recognised teacher. His answer points to the true source of his teaching: the Father.
Jesus does not deny that he teaches. He denies that the teaching is his own invention. The Son speaks what he receives from the Father, as a messenger speaks for the one who sends him.
A just verdict that looks at the truth of a matter and not at its surface. Isaiah says of the coming king that “he shall not judge by what his eyes see” (Isaiah 11:3).
vv: My teaching is not mine but his who sent me.

St Augustine draws out the paradox: the teaching of the Son is the Word of the Father, and the Son is that Word; so nothing is more his own, and yet it is wholly the Father's (Tractates on John 29, in substance).
Anyone who resolves to do the will of God will know whether the teaching is from God

Knowledge of God is not reached only by argument. The one who is ready to obey comes to understand. Augustine puts it this way: understanding is the reward of faith (Tractates on John 29, in substance).
Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.

Jesus argues as the teachers of his day argued: if circumcision, which touches one part of the body, may be done on the sabbath, how much more may a whole man be healed? Later rabbis used a similar argument to allow saving a life on the sabbath.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, sent as a man to men, speaks the words of God and completes the work of salvation that the Father gave him to do (Dei Verbum 4). The Church therefore does not treat the Gospel as one opinion among many but receives it as the teaching of the Father given in the Son. Verse 17 is also a word of encouragement for every searcher: the honest will to do what God asks is already a door to faith.

qa: Did God really want Abraham to kill his son?

The story itself says that God was testing Abraham (Genesis 22:1), and God stops his hand. In a world where some peoples offered children to their gods, the story teaches the opposite: the God of Israel does not want human sacrifice, and he himself provides the offering. For Christians it points to the one sacrifice God did not withhold, the gift of his own Son, which no human father was asked to make.
study: The patriarchs blessed a future they would not see. What blessing am I handing on to the next generation in my family and parish?
Jesus says that whoever is ready to do God's will shall know his teaching. Is there something God is asking of me that I am delaying, and could that be why I find faith hard?

lead: Today's readings speak of what we receive and from whom. Paul thanks the Philippians for the gifts they sent him, and calls their generosity “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God”, adding that God will supply every need of theirs. In John, Jesus tells his opponents that the one who is from God hears the words of God. A gift given in love rises to God like incense; a word received with an open heart shows whose children we are. The key words are offering and hearing.

r.h: A fragrant offering, pleasing to God
set: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. Many scholars place the letter in Rome around AD 61–62; others think of an earlier imprisonment at Ephesus. Philippi was the first church he founded in Europe (Acts 16), and it remained especially close to him. The Philippians had sent him help by Epaphroditus, who fell gravely ill while with Paul and then returned home with this letter (2:25–30).

Our verses close the letter's thanksgiving for that gift (4:10–20). Just before them Paul says that he has learned to be content in plenty and in want, and that he can do all things through him who strengthens him (4:11–13). So he thanks them warmly, yet without making his peace depend on their money.
str: vv. 15–16: the Philippians alone shared with him from the beginning, even at Thessalonica.
v. 17: not the gift but the fruit that grows to their account.
v. 18: the gift as a fragrant sacrifice to God.
vv. 19–20: God will supply their every need; a doxology.
kw: in the matter of giving and receiving
The language of business accounts. Paul uses a merchant's words to describe a partnership in the Gospel: they gave material help, he gave them the word of God, and both shared in one work.
I have been paid in full
The word written on ancient receipts, meaning “received in full”. With a smile Paul gives the Philippians a receipt for their gift.

The Greek Old Testament uses these words for sacrifices that rise as a pleasing smell before the Lord (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9). Ephesians 5:2 uses them of Christ's own self-offering. Gifts to the poor and to the Church's mission share in that worship.
vv: Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the profit that accumulates to your account.
The giver gains more than the one who receives. Paul is glad, not for his own comfort, but because their love is bearing fruit before God.
a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God.
A gift of money sent to a prisoner is called a sacrifice. Christian worship is not shut up in the sanctuary; it flows from the altar into acts of love, which in turn are offered back to God.
And my God will fully satisfy every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
Paul cannot repay them, but his God can. The same verb was used in verse 18: “I am fully satisfied”. As God has filled Paul through them, he will fill them.
ch: The Church teaches that the faithful are obliged to help with the material needs of the Church, each according to his means (CCC 2043). Philippians shows the spirit of that duty: not a tax but a share in the Gospel, a sacrifice pleasing to God. Gifts given for priests, missionaries, catechists and the poor are part of the offering that the faithful bring to the Holy Qurbono, where all our gifts are joined to the one sacrifice of Christ.

r.h: Whoever is from God hears the words of God
set: John 8 records a long and sharp dispute during the feast of Booths. The part that leads to our verses begins with Jesus speaking to “the Jews who had believed in him” (8:31–32): “If you continue in my word, you are truly my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” His hearers protest that they are children of Abraham and have never been slaves (8:33). The conversation turns on the question of fatherhood: who is your real father, shown by what you do?

These words must be read with great care. They were spoken in a particular quarrel to particular opponents who, the text says, were seeking to kill Jesus (8:40). They are not a judgment on the Jewish people. The Church teaches that what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
str: v. 42: if God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God.
v. 43: why you cannot understand: you cannot hear my word.
v. 44: your deeds show another father: the devil, murderer and liar.
vv. 45–47: I tell the truth; who can convict me of sin? Whoever is from God hears God's words.
kw: In John to be “from” someone is to have one's origin and nature from him. Jesus came from God; those who are born of God (1:13) recognise the voice of their Father in him.

Literally “man-killer”. The book of Wisdom says that “through the devil's envy death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24). The devil was a murderer from the beginning because he led humanity into sin and death.
The opposite of truth, which in John is not just correct information but the reality of God revealed in Jesus (14:6). The devil's first word in Scripture was a lie about God (Genesis 3:4–5).
vv: If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and now I am here.
Love is the proof of kinship. Those who belong to the Father love the Son whom he has sent.
Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot accept my word.
Literally “you cannot hear my word”. Not understanding is a matter of the heart before it is a matter of the mind.
Whoever is from God hears the words of God.
A test that applies to every reader of the Gospel, not only to the hearers that day. Each of us shows whose child we are by how we receive the word of God.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 44 when it speaks of the fallen angel: Scripture witnesses to the disastrous influence of the one Jesus calls “a murderer from the beginning” (CCC 394). It quotes it again when it teaches that lying is a direct offence against the truth: the Lord denounces lying as the work of the devil (CCC 2482). The Church reads this hard passage as a warning to every believer, including Christians: the children of God are known by love of the Son and by truthfulness, not by descent or name alone.

qa: Did Jesus call the Jewish people children of the devil?

No. Jesus, his mother and his apostles were Jews, and he loved his people. In John 8 he speaks to opponents in a heated dispute and judges deeds, not birth: those who seek to kill an innocent man and reject the truth are doing the work of the murderer and liar. The Church firmly rejects any use of these words against the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The warning is meant for every reader, Christian or not, who closes his ears to God's word.
study: Paul calls a gift of money “a fragrant offering”. How might my giving to the parish, the missions and the poor become an act of worship and not only a duty?
Jesus says that whoever is from God hears his words. When I listen to the Gospel at the Holy Qurbono, what helps me really to hear, and what blocks my ears?

lead: On the Sixth Sunday after Pentecost the readings speak of a God who gathers. In the evening Gospel (Luke 17:1–10) Jesus warns against causing others to stumble, commands forgiveness “seven times a day”, and answers the apostles' plea “Increase our faith!” with the mustard seed and the servant who says, “We are worthless slaves; we have done only what we ought to have done!” In Exodus 30:34–38 the Lord gives Moses the recipe for the holy incense, “pure and holy”, to be placed before the covenant in the tent of meeting. Psalm 20 prays for the king: “Some take pride in chariots, and some in horses, but our pride is in the name of the Lord our God.” In Isaiah 14:22–27 the Lord of hosts swears that his plan against Babylon and Assyria shall stand: “His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back?” In Acts 17:22–34 Paul preaches at the Areopagus in Athens about the unknown God, in whom “we live and move and have our being”.

We study three readings more closely. In 2 Samuel, Abner, the commander of Saul's house and David's old enemy, comes to Hebron to bring all Israel to David; David makes a feast for him and sends him away in peace. Paul tells the Corinthians that they are one body with many members, where the weaker parts are indispensable and every member suffers and rejoices with the others. In Luke, Jesus answers those who grumble because he eats with sinners with the parable of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one lost sheep. The key words are gathering, body and joy.

r.h: Abner makes peace with David
set: After the death of Saul, David was anointed king over Judah at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:4), while Abner, Saul's army commander, made Saul's son Ishbaal (called Ish-bosheth in many translations) king over the northern tribes. “There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David” (3:1). Abner was the real power in the north, but after a bitter quarrel with Ishbaal (3:6–11) he decided to change sides and offered David his help “to bring all Israel over to you” (3:12).

Our verses tell how Abner prepares the elders of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, Saul's own tribe, and then comes to David. The story does not end happily: on his way back Abner is murdered by Joab in revenge for his brother (3:27). David mourns him publicly, and “all Israel understood that day that the king had no part in the killing” (3:37). The unity of the kingdom will be reached only in chapter 5, when all the tribes come to Hebron and anoint David.
str: vv. 17–18: Abner tells the elders of Israel to make David king, recalling the Lord's promise.
v. 19: he speaks to Benjamin and goes to David at Hebron.
v. 20: David makes a feast for Abner and his twenty men.
v. 21: Abner promises to rally all Israel to a covenant; David sends him away in peace.
¶ The phrase “in peace” is repeated three times in verses 21–23, as if to underline how fragile that peace was.
kw: The elders “have been seeking David as king”. The people already sensed where God's choice lay. Abner only brings to the surface a longing that was there.

Literally “by the hand of David my servant”. No oracle in exactly these words is recorded earlier in Samuel, but the title “my servant David” becomes central in the prophets (Ezekiel 34:23) and points ahead to the Messiah.
More than the absence of war: wholeness, right relationship. The meal and the peaceful farewell show reconciliation between former enemies, a peace that sin will soon wound.
vv: For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you.
God's purpose ripens slowly. David does not seize the throne of Israel by force; he waits until the people come to him.
Through my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines, and from all their enemies.
The deliverer is called a servant. Kingship in Israel is service of God and of his people, a pattern fulfilled in Christ, who came “not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).
David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him.
Reconciliation is sealed at a table. A shared meal was a sign of peace and covenant in the ancient world.
So David dismissed Abner, and he went away in peace.
David receives his former enemy without revenge. The violence that follows comes from Joab, not from the king.
ch: The Fathers saw in David the shepherd-king a figure of Christ, the Son of David, who gathers into one the scattered children of God (John 11:52). The Catechism calls David “par excellence the king after God's own heart”, the shepherd who prays for his people (CCC 2579). Today's passage teaches that God's kingdom grows through reconciliation: a former enemy is received, a feast is shared, peace is offered. It also warns, through Joab's crime, how easily the old spirit of revenge can destroy what grace has begun.

r.h: Many members, one body
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, probably around AD 53–55, to a gifted but divided community. Some boasted of their spiritual gifts, especially speaking in tongues, and looked down on others (chapters 12–14). Paul answers by recalling that there are varieties of gifts but the same Spirit (12:4), and then uses the image of the body.

The comparison of a city or a people with a body was well known in the ancient world. The Roman historian Livy tells how Menenius Agrippa persuaded the common people of Rome to end a revolt with a fable about the limbs that refused to feed the stomach (Livy 2.32). Paul goes further: the Church is not only like a body; it is the body of Christ (12:27).
str: vv. 12–13: one body, many members: all baptized in one Spirit.
vv. 14–20: no member may say “I do not belong”.
vv. 21–24: no member may say “I have no need of you”; the weaker are indispensable.
vv. 25–26: one care for all: suffering and rejoicing together.
kw: The word Paul also uses of the Eucharist: “The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (10:16–17). The body of Christ received at the altar builds the body of Christ which is the Church.
we were baptized… we were made to drink
Two images of the one Spirit: plunged into him in Baptism, given him to drink as water. Many interpreters hear in the second an echo of the Spirit as living water (John 7:37–39).
A single Greek word: to suffer with. Paul's own compassion for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28–29) is this word made flesh.
vv: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.
Paul does not say “so it is with the Church”, but “so it is with Christ”. Christ and his members form one body, the whole Christ, as St Augustine loved to say.
For in the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body

The verse goes on: “Jews or Greeks, slaves or free”. Paul names the deepest divisions of his world, of race and of status, and declares them overcome in Baptism. No caste or class divides the body of Christ.
On the contrary, the members of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable,
The word “seem” matters. The sick, the old, the poor and the little ones only seem weaker. In God's eyes they are necessary to the body.
If one member suffers, all suffer together with it; if one member is honored, all rejoice together with it.
The test of a living parish: the sorrow of one family is felt by all, and the joy of one is shared by all.
ch: The Second Vatican Council takes up this chapter to describe the Church as the body of Christ, in which the Spirit gives a diversity of gifts, and from which it follows that if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it (Lumen Gentium 7; CCC 791). Pope Pius XII wrote a whole encyclical on this theme, Mystici Corporis (1943). St Augustine told the newly baptized at Easter that if they are the body of Christ and his members, it is their own mystery that is placed on the Lord's table, and they receive their own mystery (Sermon 272, in substance).

r.h: The lost sheep
set: Luke 15 is the heart of Luke's Gospel of mercy. It contains three parables of the lost: the sheep, the coin and the two sons. All three answer the same complaint, given in verses 1–2: tax collectors and sinners come to hear Jesus, and some of the Pharisees and scribes grumble that he welcomes them and eats with them.

The Pharisees were devout men who wanted all Israel to live in holiness, and they took great care about table fellowship, because eating together meant belonging together. Luke also tells of Pharisees who invited Jesus to dine (7:36; 14:1). The parable is not an attack on them but an invitation: come and share the shepherd's joy. Matthew gives a similar parable in a different setting, about the care of the little ones in the community (Matthew 18:12–14).
str: vv. 1–2: sinners draw near; the righteous grumble.
v. 3: Jesus answers with a parable.
v. 4: the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine and seeks the one until he finds it.
vv. 5–6: he carries it home on his shoulders and calls his friends to rejoice.
v. 7: more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.
kw: The word recalls Israel murmuring against Moses and the Lord in the wilderness (Exodus 16:2–8 in the Greek Old Testament). Grumbling is the sound of a heart that does not understand God's mercy.
To receive someone, as a host receives a guest. The complaint is true: Jesus does welcome sinners. What his critics see as a scandal is the Gospel itself.
The same word returns at the end of the chapter: the son “was lost and has been found” (15:24, 32). In Luke, Jesus says that “the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost” (19:10).
vv: This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.
Meant as an accusation, it is a perfect summary of the ministry of Jesus. It is also a description of the Holy Qurbono, where the Lord still welcomes sinners and feeds them at his table.
does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that is lost until he finds it?
“Until he finds it”: the shepherd does not give up. God's search for us is patient and stubborn.
When he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders and rejoices.

No scolding, no punishment, only joy. The shepherd carries the weight himself. One of the earliest images of Christ in Christian art, found in the catacombs of Rome, is the young shepherd with a sheep on his shoulders.
there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
The “ninety-nine righteous” are a gentle irony. No one really needs no repentance. The joy of heaven is offered to all who are willing to be found.
ch: The Catechism points to Jesus receiving sinners at his table as a gesture that expresses in an astonishing way both God's forgiveness and the return to the bosom of the People of God (CCC 1443), and it teaches that the Gospel is the revelation in Jesus Christ of God's mercy to sinners, as the parables of Luke 15 show (CCC 1846). St Gregory the Great, preaching on this parable, says that the shepherd laid the sheep on his shoulders because Christ took our human nature and bore our sins (Homilies on the Gospels 34, in substance). The parable stands behind every confessional: the sacrament of Reconciliation is the shepherd carrying the sheep home.

qa: Is it fair to leave ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness to look for one?

The parable is not a lesson in sheep farming. It shows the heart of God, for whom no one is a mere number. The question in verse 4, “Which one of you…?”, invites the hearers to admit that they too would search for something precious. If we do that for a sheep, how much more does God do it for a person? The ninety-nine are not abandoned; the whole flock is safer for having a shepherd who never gives up on anyone.
Paul says the members are many but the body is one. Does that mean everyone in the Church must be the same?

No. Unity is not sameness. The eye and the hand are different and must remain different, or the body cannot live. The Church holds together many rites, languages and gifts, and this variety is a richness, not a threat, as long as all are joined in the one faith, the sacraments and communion with the successors of the apostles (CCC 814–815).
Abner was a former enemy with mixed motives. Why does David receive him?

David trusts that God's plan for Israel can work even through imperfect people. He does not demand that Abner first prove pure intentions; he offers a feast and peace. Christ goes further still: he receives sinners not because they have earned it but so that they may be changed. Reconciliation always involves the risk of trusting someone who once wronged us.
rite: We keep this Sunday within the Apostles' Fast, which ends with the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on Tuesday. The readings suit the season: the apostles ask for faith in the evening Gospel, Paul preaches at Athens, and the parable of the lost sheep shows what kind of shepherds the apostles were sent to be. In the West Syriac tradition incense surrounds the prayers of the Holy Qurbono and of the hours, especially the Sedro, the long prayer that is said while the incense rises. Exodus 30 gives the background: the incense is holy, offered before the Lord, a sign of prayer rising to God (Psalm 141:2). When the censer swings in our churches, it reminds us that the whole Church, many members and one body, rises together before God, and that the Shepherd who found us carries us there.
study: David receives his former enemy with a feast and sends him away in peace. Is there someone with whom I need to share a meal of reconciliation?
Paul says no member can say “I have no need of you”. Whom in my parish or family have I treated as unnecessary, and how can I honour them?
The shepherd carries the lost sheep home on his shoulders. When did I last let Christ carry me home in the sacrament of Reconciliation?
Jesus' critics grumbled because he ate with sinners. When I see someone return to the Church, do I grumble or do I rejoice?

lead: Both readings are about the word that is handed on and the fruit it bears. Paul tells Timothy to avoid quarrels about words and to be “a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly explaining the word of truth.” In John, Jesus reminds the disciples that they did not choose him; he chose them and appointed them to bear fruit that will last, and the fruit he names is love for one another. On the day the Panchangam remembers Mar Irenaeus, the readings fit a bishop who spent his life explaining the word of truth rightly. The key words are truth and fruit.

r.h: Rightly explaining the word of truth
set: 2 Timothy is written as Paul's last letter, from prison in Rome, to his beloved co-worker Timothy, who was leading the church at Ephesus. Many scholars think that the Pastoral Letters were written by a disciple in Paul's name after his death; others hold that they come from Paul himself near the end of his life. The Church receives them as inspired Scripture either way.

Just before our verses comes the hymn: “If we have died with him, we will also live with him” (2:11). Timothy must remind the community of this saving faith, and protect it from teachers who were spreading empty speculation; verses 17–18 name two of them, who claimed that the resurrection had already taken place.
str: v. 14: remind them; warn them not to wrangle over words.
v. 15: be an approved worker who rightly handles the word of truth.
v. 16: avoid profane chatter, which leads into impiety.
kw: Literally “to fight with words”. Not careful thought about the faith, which the Church has always needed, but quarrels for the sake of winning, which leave the listeners confused and divided.
a worker who has no need to be ashamed
The image of a labourer whose work can bear inspection. Timothy's ministry is honest work done before God, not a performance before people.
Literally “cutting straight”, like a road cut in a straight line or a furrow ploughed true. The minister of the word keeps to the straight path of the truth and leads others along it.
vv: warn them before God that they are to avoid wrangling over words, which does no good but only ruins those who are listening.
The test of any argument about faith is what it does to the listeners. Quarrels that leave people bitter or lost are not the work of the Spirit.
Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved by him, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly explaining the word of truth.
This verse has become a motto for preachers and catechists. The first audience of every preacher is God.
Avoid profane chatter, for it will lead people into more and more impiety,

The same warning appears at the close of 1 Timothy: “Avoid the profane chatter and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge” (1 Timothy 6:20). Empty talk does not stay empty; it pulls people away from God.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the task of authentically interpreting the word of God has been entrusted to the living teaching office of the Church, which is not above the word of God but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on (Dei Verbum 10; CCC 86). St Irenaeus, remembered today, did exactly what this reading asks. Against teachers who claimed a secret knowledge, he pointed to the faith publicly handed down from the apostles through the bishops of the churches, above all the church of Rome, with which, he wrote, every church must agree (Against Heresies 3.3; CCC 834).

r.h: You did not choose me but I chose you
set: These verses belong to the Last Supper discourse. Jesus has spoken of himself as the true vine and of the disciples as branches (15:1–8), and has told them: “No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends” (15:13). He no longer calls them servants but friends (15:15). Now he tells them where their calling comes from and what it is for.
str: v. 16a: the initiative is his: I chose you.
v. 16b: you are appointed to go and bear lasting fruit; the Father will give what you ask in my name.
v. 17: the purpose of the commands: love one another.
kw: In the ancient world a disciple chose his teacher. Here the Teacher chooses. Every vocation begins in the unearned love of Christ, not in our own merit or plan.
Literally “I placed” or “I set”. The same verb is used when the good shepherd “lays down” his life (10:11). The one who lays down his life for his friends also sets them in their mission.
The verb menein, to abide or remain, runs through the whole chapter. Fruit that lasts grows only on branches that abide in the vine (15:5).
vv: You did not choose me but I chose you.
A word of humility and of comfort. Humility, because no one can boast of his calling; comfort, because the one who chose us knew our weakness and still chose us.
And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last,
The disciples are not chosen to stay in the upper room but to go. The fruit is both the holiness of their lives and the people brought to Christ through them.
I am giving you these commands so that you may love one another.
All the commands come down to one. The fruit that lasts is love.
ch: The Church hears in these words the source of every vocation, especially the call of the apostles and of their successors the bishops. The Catechism teaches that Christ chose the Twelve and made them sharers in his mission (CCC 858), and that the new commandment of love sums up the whole law of the Gospel (CCC 1970). St Augustine, preaching on this passage, says that the Lord did not choose the disciples because they were good, but made them good by choosing them (Tractates on John 86, in substance).

qa: Paul says to avoid wrangling over words. Does that mean that exact words in matters of faith are unimportant?

No. The Church has always cared about the right words: the Creed, the definitions of the councils, the words of the sacraments. What Paul condemns is quarrelling for its own sake, clever debate that serves pride and leaves the hearers worse off. Careful words that guard the truth are a service of love; empty arguments are not. St Irenaeus fought hard for the true faith, but always so that ordinary believers might keep it clearly and simply.
rite: The Panchangam remembers Mar Irenaeus today, the day on which the wider Church keeps the memory of St Irenaeus of Lyons. Born in Asia Minor around AD 130, he heard as a young man the preaching of St Polycarp of Smyrna, who had known the apostle John. He became bishop of Lyons in Gaul and wrote Against Heresies, the great defence of the apostolic faith against those who claimed secret knowledge. His name means “peaceful”, and he lived up to it, pleading with Pope Victor for peace among the churches in the dispute over the date of Easter. He taught that “the glory of God is man fully alive, and the life of man is the vision of God” (Against Heresies 4.20.7; CCC 294). In 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church with the title “Doctor of Unity”. A Church that holds the faith of the apostles and longs for the unity of all Christians can pray today with him.
study: Paul tells Timothy to be a worker who need not be ashamed before God. In conversations about faith at home or online, do I seek to win, or to help the other person come closer to the truth?
Jesus says, “You did not choose me but I chose you.” How does knowing that Christ chose me change the way I look at my own vocation and my weaknesses?

lead: On the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul the readings trace the path of two men whom Christ called by name, sent out, and brought at last to martyrdom in Rome. The evening Gospel (Matthew 16:13–20) gives Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God”, and the Lord's reply, “you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.” In Genesis 12:1–8 the Lord calls Abram to leave his country for a land he will be shown, and Abram goes. Proverbs 13:1–9 praises the one who listens to correction and guards his mouth. In Daniel 1:1–9 the young Daniel, taken to Babylon, resolves not to defile himself with the king's food, faithful to God in a foreign capital. In Acts 12:6–19, while “the church prayed fervently to God for him” (12:5, just before the reading), an angel leads Peter out of Herod's prison and the chains fall from his wrists.

We study three readings more closely. In Isaiah the Lord says to his people in exile, “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.” In 2 Timothy, Paul, facing death, looks back: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” In John, the risen Lord asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?”, entrusts his flock to him, and foretells the death by which he would glorify God. The key words are called by name, poured out and love.

r.h: I have called you by name, you are mine
set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC. Many scholars think these chapters come from a prophet of the exile who continued the tradition of Isaiah of Jerusalem. They open with the cry “Comfort, O comfort my people” (40:1) and are full of tender promises.

Just before our passage the prophet has told the people that their suffering came because they did not walk in God's ways (42:24–25). Then, with the words “But now”, the tone changes completely. God does not cast off his sinful people. He reminds them that he created them, redeemed them and called them by name, and he promises to gather their children from every direction of the earth.
str: v. 1: do not fear: I created you, I redeemed you, I called you by name.
v. 2: through water and fire, I will be with you.
vv. 3–4: you are precious in my sight; I give nations as your ransom.
vv. 5–7: do not fear: I will gather your sons and daughters from east and west, north and south.
kw: From gā’al, the duty of the next of kin, the gō’ēl, who buys back a relative sold into slavery or a family field that was lost (Leviticus 25:25). God acts as Israel's nearest kinsman.
I have called you by name
To call by name is to know personally, to choose and to claim. God names his people as a father names a child.
The price paid to release someone. The language is poetic: the Lord says no price is too high for his people. Christians hear it fulfilled when Jesus gives “his life a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).
vv: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.
“Do not fear” comes twice in the passage (vv. 1, 5). The ground of courage is not our strength but God's claim on us.
When you pass through the waters, I will be with you;
Israel remembered the Red Sea and the Jordan. Christian readers have heard here a promise for Baptism: God brings his people through the waters, not around them.
Because you are precious in my sight, and honored, and I love you,
One of the most tender verses of the Old Testament. God's love does not depend on Israel's worth; it gives Israel its worth.
everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed and made.
The goal of the gathering is God's glory. A people called by God's name exists to show his goodness to the world.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God calls each one by name and that everyone's name is sacred (CCC 2158), and that in Baptism the Christian receives his name in the Church (CCC 2156). On the feast of Peter and Paul these verses take on a special colour. Jesus gave Simon a new name, Peter (Matthew 16:18), and called Saul on the Damascus road by his own name (Acts 9:4). Neither was chosen for his perfection: Peter would deny the Lord, and Paul had persecuted the Church. Both were redeemed, called by name, and made precious instruments of God's glory.

r.h: I have fought the good fight
set: These verses read as Paul's farewell. In the letter he is a prisoner in Rome, abandoned by many, awaiting the end. Many scholars think that the Pastoral Letters were written after Paul's death by a disciple in his name, drawing on his memory and perhaps on his notes; others hold that Paul wrote them himself. Either way, the Church has always heard in this passage the authentic voice of the apostle's last witness.

Ancient tradition, going back to St Clement of Rome at the end of the first century (1 Clement 5), tells that Peter and Paul both bore witness by their death in Rome under the emperor Nero, in the 60s AD. Paul, a Roman citizen, was beheaded, tradition says, on the road to Ostia, where the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls now stands.
str: v. 6: my life is being poured out; the time of departure has come.
v. 7: three verbs in the perfect tense: fought, finished, kept.
v. 8: the crown of righteousness, for me and for all who long for his appearing.
vv. 9–10: come quickly: Demas has deserted me; others are away.
kw: I am being poured out as a libation
A drink offering of wine poured out at the altar (Numbers 28:7). Paul sees his coming death as an act of worship. He used the same image years earlier in Philippians 2:17.
The word for loosing a ship from its moorings or striking a tent. Death is not an end for Paul but a setting out.
Not a king's diadem but the wreath given to the winner of a race. Paul has run the course; the Lord, the righteous judge, will give the prize.
vv: As for me, I am already being poured out as a libation, and the time of my departure has come.
Paul's death is joined to the sacrifice of Christ. The martyr does not merely suffer; he offers.
I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
The first two images come from the games, the third from a steward's duty. Faith is a treasure entrusted to him, and he hands it on intact.
From now on there is reserved for me the crown of righteousness,
The crown is “not only to me but also to all who have longed for his appearing”. Paul's hope is not private. Every faithful Christian shares in it.
for Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me
Demas had been Paul's co-worker (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24). The apostle's last days were lonely. Even great saints know the pain of being abandoned.
ch: The Church teaches that our merit before God comes from the fact that God has freely chosen to associate us with the work of his grace (CCC 2008). The crown is truly given for the race that was run, yet the strength to run was God's gift. St Augustine, reflecting on this passage, says that when God crowns our merits he crowns his own gifts (in substance). Paul's words have comforted dying Christians for centuries, and they are fitting for priests and religious who have served long and faithfully: the fight was hard, the race long, but the faith was kept.

r.h: Feed my sheep
set: John 21 is an epilogue to the Gospel. The risen Jesus appears by the Sea of Tiberias to seven disciples who have gone back to fishing. After a night with no catch, at his word they haul in a net full of fish, and on the shore he has prepared a charcoal fire with fish and bread (21:9). The Greek word for that charcoal fire, anthrakia, appears only one other time in the New Testament: at the fire in the high priest's courtyard where Peter warmed himself and denied Jesus (18:18).
So by a charcoal fire the denial is healed. Three times Peter had denied being his disciple; three times now the Lord asks, “Do you love me?”
str: v. 15: first question: “more than these?”; feed my lambs.
v. 16: second question; tend my sheep.
v. 17: third question; Peter is hurt; “Lord, you know everything”; feed my sheep.
vv. 18–19: Peter will stretch out his hands and be led where he does not wish to go; “Follow me.”
kw: do you love me… I love you

John alternates two Greek verbs for love. Many scholars think the change is a matter of style. Others, including Pope Benedict XVI in a general audience of 2006, saw in it Jesus coming down to the measure of Peter's humbled love, until the third time he asks in Peter's own word.

To feed is to give food; to tend is the whole work of a shepherd: to guide, protect and govern. The Greek also alternates between lambs and sheep. The whole flock, small and grown, is entrusted to Peter.
you will stretch out your hands
Early Christian writers, among them Tertullian, understood this as a reference to crucifixion. Verse 19 confirms that Jesus was speaking of the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God.
vv: Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?
Jesus calls him by his old name, Simon, as at their first meeting (1:42). Before Peter can feed the flock, his own heart must be made new.
Peter felt hurt because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?”
The third question touches the deepest wound. Peter no longer boasts, as he did at the Supper (13:37). He simply appeals to the Lord's knowledge of his heart.
Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.
Peter's love now rests not on his own strength but on Christ's knowledge. This is the humility from which true authority in the Church is born.
After this he said to him, “Follow me.”
The first call by the lake (Mark 1:17) is renewed. This time Peter knows where following will lead: to the cross.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus entrusted a specific authority to Peter, the power of the keys, and that after his resurrection the Good Shepherd confirmed this mandate: “Feed my sheep” (CCC 553). The office of Peter continues in the Bishop of Rome, the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful (Lumen Gentium 23; CCC 882).
