The Catechism also sees in Peter's conversion after his threefold denial a witness to the mercy of Jesus' look (CCC 1429). The one who holds the keys is a forgiven sinner, and the authority he receives is the authority of love.

qa: Is the “rock” Peter himself or Peter's faith?

The Fathers explored both, and the two do not compete. The Catechism says that Christ built his Church on the rock of the faith confessed by St Peter (CCC 424), and also that he made Simon, whom he named Peter, the rock of his Church and gave him the keys (CCC 552, 881). Jesus speaks to Peter in person: “you are Peter”. The man and his confession belong together. Peter is the rock because the Father revealed to him who Jesus is, and he remains the rock by holding fast to that faith and strengthening his brothers in it (Luke 22:32).
Peter and Paul once disagreed sharply at Antioch. Why are they honoured on the same day?

Paul tells of that disagreement himself (Galatians 2:11–14), and he also tells how James, Cephas and John gave him “the right hand of fellowship” (Galatians 2:9). They had different missions, Peter to the circumcised and Paul to the Gentiles, but one faith and one Lord. St Augustine preached that the two apostles share one feast because they were one, and though they suffered on different days, they were as one (Sermon 295, in substance). Their feast teaches that unity in the Church is not uniformity of temperament but communion in the truth and in love.
Peter denied Jesus three times. How could he still be made shepherd of the whole Church?

Because Christ's choice rests on grace, not on our record. Peter's fall taught him humility, and his restoration taught him mercy. Jesus had already prayed that Peter's faith would not fail, and told him, “when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). A shepherd who has himself been forgiven knows how to seek the lost. The Church's authority comes from Christ, not from the personal perfection of the one who holds it.
rite: Today the Apostles' Fast comes to its end with the feast of the two great apostles. The West Syriac tradition, to which our Church belongs, has always looked to Peter with special love, for ancient tradition holds that he presided over the church of Antioch before going to Rome, and Antioch was where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26). Paul too was sent out from Antioch on his missionary journeys (Acts 13:1–3). In 1930 the Malankara Catholic Church entered into full communion with the successor of Peter in Rome, and today, in praying for the Pope, we give thanks for that gift. We pray also with our brothers and sisters of the Orthodox Churches, who honour Peter and Paul with the same devotion, that the Lord may bring all his flock into one fold under the one Shepherd (John 10:16).
study: God says, “I have called you by name, you are mine.” How does my own baptismal name remind me of God's personal love and call?
Paul could say at the end, “I have kept the faith.” What helps me guard the faith I received, and what am I doing to hand it on whole to my children?
Jesus healed Peter's threefold denial with a threefold question of love. Is there a failure in my life that the Lord wants to heal not by forgetting it but by asking me again, “Do you love me?”
How can our family and parish pray more faithfully for the Pope, for our bishops, and for the unity of all Christians?

lead: The day after the feast of Peter and Paul, the Church honours all twelve apostles together. In Mark, Jesus goes up the mountain, calls those whom he wants, and appoints twelve “to be with him, and to be sent out to proclaim the message”. In 2 Corinthians, Paul shows what that sending looked like in real life: hardships, beatings, sleepless nights, and through it all a strange wealth, “as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.” The key words are with him and sent.

r.h: As having nothing, and yet possessing everything
set: In 2 Corinthians Paul defends his ministry before a community where some questioned whether he was a true apostle. Just before our passage he has said that God has given him “the ministry of reconciliation” and that “we are ambassadors for Christ” (5:18–20). Now he urges the Corinthians not to let God's grace go to waste, and describes the life of a servant of God.

The list of sufferings is a form known in the ancient world, where philosophers listed the trials they had endured to show their steadiness. Paul uses it in his own way: his endurance proves not his own strength but the power of God at work in weakness (compare 4:7–12; 11:23–29).
str: vv. 1–2: do not accept God's grace in vain: now is the day of salvation.
v. 3: no obstacle in anyone's way.
vv. 4–5: endurance in afflictions, beatings, labours, hunger.
vv. 6–7: purity, knowledge, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love, the power of God.
vv. 8–10: a chain of paradoxes: dying, and see, we are alive.
kw: Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8 and then declares its fulfilment: “See, now is the acceptable time.” Kairos is not clock time but the decisive moment, God's moment, which must be seized.
The apostles are not masters of the faithful but servants of God for them. The word diakonos means one who serves at table or carries out another's errand.
The pattern of verses 8–10: what the world sees, and what God sees. The apostle seems unknown, dying, sorrowful, poor; in truth he is known, alive, rejoicing and rich.
vv: As we work together with him, we urge you also not to accept the grace of God in vain.
Grace is never forced on anyone. It can be received in vain, like seed that falls on rocky ground. Paul calls himself God's co-worker in bringing it to fruit.
See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!
The Catechism uses this verse when it teaches that the message of the Last Judgment calls us to conversion while God still gives us the acceptable time (CCC 1041).
as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.
The apostles left everything to follow Christ (Mark 10:28), and in him they possessed all things. Their poverty enriched the whole world with the Gospel.
ch: The Catechism uses Paul's words to describe the apostles and their successors: they are ministers of the new covenant, servants of God, ambassadors for Christ, stewards of the mysteries of God (CCC 859). Their ministry belongs to Christ, who acts through them. These verses fit ordinations of priests and bishops and the feasts of apostles, as a mirror held up to every minister: endurance, purity, kindness, genuine love, and joy in the midst of trial.

r.h: He appointed twelve
set: Up to this point in Mark, Jesus has called a few disciples one by one by the Sea of Galilee (1:16–20; 2:14), healed many, and met growing opposition (3:6). Now, on a mountain, he forms the group of the Twelve. The mountain recalls Sinai, where God formed his people Israel, and the number twelve recalls the twelve tribes. Jesus is gathering the renewed people of God.

The list of the Twelve appears four times in the New Testament (Matthew 10:2–4; Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13). Peter is always first and Judas Iscariot, where he appears, always last. Some names differ: Mark's Thaddaeus seems to be the same as Luke's “Judas son of James”.
str: v. 13: on the mountain he calls those whom he wants; they come.
vv. 14–15: he appoints twelve: to be with him, to be sent to preach, to have authority over demons.
vv. 16–19: the names, with Simon renamed Peter and the sons of Zebedee named Boanerges.
kw: Literally “he made twelve”. The Greek verb is the one used in Genesis for God's creating. Jesus does not find the Twelve ready made; he makes them into what they are to be.
The first purpose of the call, before any work. An apostle is first a companion of Jesus. Only those who have been with him can be sent to speak of him.

The root of the word “apostle”: one who is sent with the authority of the sender. In verse 14 Mark adds that Jesus “also named” them apostles. The Syriac word shliha, used in our liturgy for an apostle, also means “one who is sent”.
vv: He went up the mountain and called to him those whom he wanted, and they came to him.
The call depends on his will, not on their qualifications. Their part is simply to come.
And he appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, to be with him, and to be sent out to proclaim the message,

Being with and being sent belong together. Prayer without mission becomes closed; mission without prayer becomes empty. Some manuscripts lack the words “whom he also named apostles”, but the NRSV keeps them.
and Thomas,
The apostle whom our ancient tradition in India honours as the one who first brought the Gospel to our land. Every list of the Twelve names him.
and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
Even the list of the chosen ends in sorrow. The call of Christ is real, but so is human freedom.
ch: The Catechism teaches that from the beginning of his public life Jesus chose certain men, twelve in number, to be with him and to share in his mission, and gave them a share in his authority (CCC 551). Representing the twelve tribes of Israel, they are the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem (CCC 765; Revelation 21:14). The bishops, as successors of the apostles, continue their mission until the end of time (Lumen Gentium 20).

qa: Why did Jesus choose Judas, if he knew he would betray him?

The Gospels do not fully explain this mystery. They show that Jesus called Judas truly, gave him the same share in the mission as the others, and kept offering him friendship even at the Supper (John 13:26). Judas was not created to betray; he freely turned away. His story warns every disciple that being chosen does not remove the need to stay faithful, and it shows that Christ's love reaches even to the one who will betray him.
rite: Our Church, like some other Eastern Churches, keeps the memory of the Twelve Apostles together on the day after the feast of Peter and Paul. It is a feast of the whole apostolic foundation of the Church, the faith we confess when we say in the Creed that the Church is “apostolic”. For the Christians of India it has a special warmth: our forefathers in faith, according to our ancient tradition, received the Gospel through Mar Thoma, the apostle Thomas, who is named among the Twelve in today's Gospel. Today we thank God for the apostles' witness, and pray for our bishops, their successors, that they may be “with him” in prayer and faithful in being sent.
study: Jesus called the Twelve first “to be with him”. How much time do I give simply to being with the Lord, before I try to do things for him?
Paul describes himself “as having nothing, and yet possessing everything”. What would it mean for me to be rich in Christ even when I lack what the world values?
